In the simulations, toxicity-penalized policies reduce DLT burden while unpenalized policies improve selection accuracy at the cost of greater toxicity. These results demonstrate a controllable safety--accuracy trade-off but do not establish superiority over conventional dose-finding designs.

Machine Learning.title: ATTUNE: Agentic Throughput Tuning for LLM Training
Machine Learning.summary: Training a large language model can occupy thousands of GPUs for weeks, and its speed depends on its recipe: how the model is split across GPUs, how memory is traded for compute, and which kernels and communication overlaps it uses. Finding a good recipe is still manual work for experts. Automated tuners search fixed lists of knobs and check only that a job runs, so they miss large gains and can ship changes that silently alter what the model learns. ATTUNE tunes any working recipe unattended within a GPU-hour budget. A coding agent, guided by lessons from past tuning runs, finds each run's bottleneck and changes one setting at a time, and a correctness gate outside the agent refuses changes known to alter training. ATTUNE is deployed in production at Amazon Ads, a business that reported $19.8 billion in revenue in Q2 2026. Its recipes train the models that power Amazon's Ads Agent. On three of the models it tunes, its recipes raise throughput per GPU by 1.7x on average and up to 3.9x over internal expert-tuned recipes. It also speeds up four of NVIDIA's benchmark recipes by 7-26% and held-out public recipes by up to 2.6x, and beats Bayesian optimization, random search and OptiCo, a recent LLM-agent tuner, at the same GPU-hour budget. We release ATTUNE at github.com/amazon-science/attune and OpenRecipes, a leaderboard of more than 60 verified recipes, at openrecipes.ai.
Machine Learning.comment: 23 pages, 6 figures. v3: revised text, figures and appendix

Machine Learning.title: Geometric and algebraic inference in humans and neural networks
Machine Learning.summary: Humans possess a remarkable ability to draw inferences from limited data. While some inferences are made intuitively from past experience, others require online reasoning based on novel information given in context. Here, we formalize these strategies, which we term geometric and algebraic inference, and study their computational tradeoffs in humans and neural networks. The geometric strategy gradually shapes representational geometry to reflect underlying relational structure, making subsequent inference cheap. The algebraic strategy flexibly attends to and reasons over novel relations given in context, but costs additional computation at inference time. We identify opposing signatures of these two strategies in transitive inference, a domain widely studied across species, and characterize the conditions under which each is observed. Our framework predicts that the geometric strategy should be dominant when relations are familiar, whereas the algebraic should emerge to support de novo inferences drawn in context. Multiple experiments demonstrate these opposing signatures in humans, neural networks trained from scratch, and large language models (LLMs). Causal interventions in the neural networks reveal that the geometric and algebraic strategies depend on representational geometry and selective attention mechanisms, respectively, and reproduce the effects of analogous neurobiological disruptions in humans. Our framework unifies these effects with disparate phenomena, including content effects observed in human and LLM reasoning and data-distribution effects observed in machine learning. Our findings reconcile competing views of cognitive flexibility that emphasize either representational geometry or algebraic manipulation by showing that each can have unique strengths, and can characterize different aspects of both human and neural network behavior.

Machine Learning.title: Variance Reduction Based Experience Replay for Policy Optimization
Machine Learning.summary: Effective reinforcement learning (RL) for complex stochastic systems requires leveraging historical data to improve sample efficiency and accelerate policy optimization. However, classical experience replay treats all past observations uniformly and fails to account for their varying contributions to learning. To address this limitation, we propose Variance Reduction Experience Replay (VRER), a principled framework that selectively reuses informative samples to reduce the variance of policy gradient estimates. VRER is algorithm-agnostic and can be integrated with existing policy optimization methods, yielding the sample-efficient off-policy algorithm, Policy Gradient with VRER (PG-VRER). To provide rigorous theoretical guarantees, we develop a novel analysis framework for experience replay that explicitly accounts for dependencies induced by Markovian dynamics and behavior-policy interactions. Using this framework, we establish finite-time convergence guarantees for PG-VRER and characterize a fundamental bias-variance trade-off: reusing older samples reduces gradient variance but may introduce greater estimation bias. Extensive experiments show that VRER consistently accelerates learning and outperforms state-of-the-art policy optimization algorithms

Machine Learning.title: Unlearning by Extrapolating a Shrink-and-Heal Lookahead
Machine Learning.summary: Unlearning aims to make a large language model behave like one retrained without its forget set. Prevailing likelihood-suppression objectives, however, lack an explicit forgetting target: they continually reward lower forget-set likelihood, making forgetting sensitive to the optimization budget. We address this limitation by estimating the direction toward the oracle without training it. Our key idea is to shrink the fine-tuned model toward its pre-fine-tuning weights and briefly re-learn the retain set, thereby removing the forget-specific contribution; in the linearized regime, this shrink-and-heal lookahead moves the model a fixed fraction of the way to the retrained model, its unique fixed point. Our method, SHIFT, extrapolates the lookahead's per-token changes into distillation targets and iteratively refines them. Evaluated against eleven baselines under a unified OpenUnlearning protocol, SHIFT achieves the highest aggregate score across all TOFU settings and the closest oracle alignment, 3.7x closer on average than the next-best method; on MUSE, it preserves the most retain knowledge. Under larger optimization budgets, baselines overshoot the oracle, while SHIFT remains near it, even under relearning attacks.

Machine Learning.title: Functional compatibility as a determinant of persistent neural learning
Machine Learning.summary: Neural networks can acquire new capabilities while damaging existing ones, but what determines whether new learning persists remains unclear. We identify functional compatibility, the extent to which incoming learning can coexist with behaviour that must be preserved, as an experimentally manipulable causal determinant of persistence. From identical neural states, we vary compatibility while matching unrestricted learning opportunity and imposing a common retention requirement. Persistent learning increases with compatibility across independent directions, convolutional and transformer architectures, vision and text, and a ten-seed replication. Learning rules and retention constraints determine how much compatible opportunity is retained, whereas nonlinear geometry limits the matched intervention at larger update norms. Functional compatibility therefore reframes stability-plasticity from preventing forgetting to determining which new learning can coexist with existing function and persist.

Machine Learning.title: MulTaBench: Benchmarking Multimodal Tabular Learning with Text and Image
Machine Learning.summary: Tabular Foundation Models have recently established the state of the art in supervised tabular learning, by leveraging pretraining to learn generalizable representations of numerical and categorical structured data. However, they lack native support for unstructured modalities such as text and image, and rely on frozen, pretrained embeddings to process them. On established Multimodal Tabular Learning benchmarks, we show that tuning the embeddings to the task improves performance. Existing benchmarks, however, often focus on the mere co-occurrence of modalities; this leads to high variance across datasets and masks the benefits of task-specific tuning. To address this gap, we introduce MulTaBench, a benchmark of 40 datasets, split equally between image-tabular and text-tabular tasks. We focus on predictive tasks where the modalities provide complementary predictive signal, and where generic embeddings lose critical information, necessitating Target-Aware Representations that are aligned with the task. Our experimental results demonstrate that the gains from target-aware representation tuning generalize across both text and image modalities, several tabular learners, encoder scales, and embedding dimensions. MulTaBench constitutes the largest image-tabular benchmarking effort to date, spanning high-impact domains such as healthcare and e-commerce. It is designed to enable the research of novel architectures which incorporate joint modeling and target-aware representations, paving the way for the development of novel Multimodal Tabular Foundation Models.

Machine Learning.title: On the Limits of Test-Time Compute for Self-Evaluation
Machine Learning.summary: Self-verification and aggregation have emerged as popular approaches for bridging the gap between pass@1 and pass@N. However, increasing the number of candidates does not consistently narrow the gap between final-answer accuracy and pass@N. To understand this limitation, we use ranking error to measure how reliably models distinguish their correct generations from incorrect ones. We show that ranking error admits a bias-variance decomposition, with both components shaped by algorithmic design choices and inference compute. Across our experiments, additional compute reduces variance, while bias initially decreases before approaching a plateau. Guided by this analysis, we introduce Scorpio, a simple and general method that jointly scores randomly grouped candidates. Across math, code, and puzzle benchmarks, Scorpio improves verification, tree search, and aggregation. For verification, Scorpio improves accuracy over the strongest baseline by up to 7 percentage points while matching or exceeding that baseline's peak accuracy with 17-42% lower inference cost. For tree search, using Scorpio to score partial solutions and select the final answer improves accuracy by up to 10 percentage points over prior methods. Finally, Scorpio improves the scaling of aggregation-based methods by 11 percentage points on coding tasks.

Machine Learning.title: Simulated petrological labels enable probabilistic mineralogy prediction from whole-rock geochemistry
Machine Learning.summary: Modal mineralogy, the mineral identities and abundances in rocks, guides geological studies and industrial resource extraction. While measuring modal mineralogy is time-intensive, whole-rock chemical measurements furnish elemental concentrations at higher throughput. Predicting mineralogy from elemental data, however, poses a one-to-many inverse problem, and labeled mineralogical datasets are too sparse to train on at scale. We address both challenges by simulating petrological labels that express multiple formation conditions per composition and at a scale unattainable by measurements. Nearly one million simulated labels supervise the middle component of a three-part model: a transformer encoder self-supervised on roughly 788,000 whole-rock compositions, the simulation-trained heads that predict distributions over mineral assemblages, and a recalibration layer that aligns the predictions with measured mineralogy. Zero-shot on 640 volcanic rocks, the model discriminates the presence of most mineral categories and predicts which rocks are richer in each mineral. However, the predicted abundances are systematically offset from measured values. Recalibration fit on as few as 25 labeled rocks recovers 76 percent of the likelihood improvement from fitting on the full 368-rock fitting set, while abundance error responds more slowly (11.0% zero-shot and 9.5% with the full fitting set). This work demonstrates how a machine learning model in the geochemical sciences can both leverage an imperfect simulator and mitigate its systematic biases.

Machine Learning.title: SPARK: Self-Correcting Embodied Memory via Physical Re-Observation
Machine Learning.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems have seen growing adoption in embodied settings as language-queryable memories of the environment. However, existing approaches often assume a reliable single-episode knowledge base (KB) or accumulate observations across episodes without correcting prior errors. Such errors can persist through incorrect semantic labels, inaccurate object positions, and inconsistent spatial relationships. To address this, we present SPARK, a corrective multi-episode framework for embodied RAG. After the first episode, a semantic critic flags regions of the KB, a targeted planner generates revisits, and a selective merge adds, removes, or replaces KB information based on the new observations. We evaluate SPARK on four outdoor AirSim maps under two degraded viewpoint conditions, using perception-built KBs, a visibility-constrained oracle used only for evaluation, and a fixed set of 158 embodied question answering (EQA) questions scored before and after correction. A single corrective episode improves downstream EQA on every map under both conditions while storing 13-41% fewer objects than append-only updating, with gains up to 2.7x on one map-condition pair. Extending correction through Episode 4 brings every map above the EQA performance of its undegraded reference. Ablations show that the critic's three signals each contribute to performance, that targeted revisits achieve a larger mean gain than untargeted ones under the same budget, and that selective merging achieves gains comparable to append-only updating with a smaller KB. Overall, SPARK demonstrates the value of correcting embodied memory through targeted re-observation, particularly as embodied systems scale and the risk of accumulated errors increases.

Machine Learning.title: Reasoning Consensus: Structural Ensembling of LLM Reasoning via Weighted DAG Aggregation
Machine Learning.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) reason in free-form chain-of-thought (CoT) without revealing which steps were well supported and which alternatives were rejected. In high-stakes domains, users then cannot judge if an answer rests on sound reasoning. Majority voting and multi-agent debate improve answers using model agreement, but do not expose agreement on individual steps. Reasoning Consensus (RC) extracts a typed reasoning graph from each CoT, merges equivalent steps across graphs from diverse models, and weights every step by how many chains attest to it. RC reveals this step-wise support and the varied justifications behind each answer. On 7 benchmarks across law, science, medicine, narrative reasoning and logic, RC matches majority voting and debate in accuracy (69.4% vs. 69.0-70.3%). An LLM judge prefers RC's best-supported graph to other graphs for the same answer. In a user study, participants read RC graphs faster than debate transcripts or vote tallies, and 14 of 18 preferred them for future use.

Machine Learning.title: Querying Counterfactuals on Tissue Graphs with Supervised Disentanglement
Machine Learning.summary: Tissue graph counterfactuals ask what a cell would express if its spatial neighborhood were altered, a question central to predicting cell behavior in tissues. Existing methods, however, present only specific instances of such queries. In this work, we first formalize tissue graph counterfactuals as a class of spatial interventions that either rewire connections between cells (edge perturbation) or modify the expression of their neighbors (node perturbation). We then introduce Cellina (https://cellina.readthedocs.io), a framework that uses supervised disentanglement to decompose a cell's intrinsic state from its spatial context, using the latter as a conditioning input for in-silico perturbation predictions. Across benchmarks spanning over 2.5 million spatially-resolved cells in observational and interventional screens, Cellina outperforms both spatially-informed and non-spatial competitors in in-silico perturbations, while training as fast as non-spatial methods. Moreover, we show that Cellina reveals cancer subdomains with distinct signaling programs in an unsupervised manner and enables targeted neighbor perturbation simulations.

Machine Learning.title: DEPLOY-RL: Active Boundary Discovery and Conservative Certification for Deployable Reinforcement Learning in Safety-Critical Continuous Processes
Machine Learning.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) policies often outperform classical controllers in simulation, yet rarely reach production in safety-critical processes. The barrier is that there is no principled way to answer "Is this policy safe to deploy?" with statistical guarantees. We introduce DEPLOY-RL, a post-training certification framework built on one key insight: deployment certification requires discovering where failures occur (boundary discovery), not measuring how much everywhere (uniform reconstruction). Our contributions: (1) a contract-coupled acquisition function that concentrates sampling on certification-critical boundaries, achieving approximately 2x sample efficiency with a semi-empirical ambiguity reduction bound (domain-calibrated convergence guarantee); (2) conformal risk control providing finite-sample false-go guarantees (<= alpha) under explicit deployment contracts; (3) a three-way decision framework (Deploy/No-Deploy/Abstain) with fail-safe PID/MPC fallback. In simulations on papermaking (industrial digital twin) and Tennessee Eastman (public benchmark), DEPLOY-RL achieves 4.4% false-go rate (vs. 8.6% for the best baseline) while retaining 88.6% policy coverage, the only method achieving <5% false-go with >85% coverage among 14 baselines under our evaluation protocol.
Machine Learning.comment: 8 pages; published in IJCAI-ECAI 2026, AI4Tech track. This version adds a publication notice

Machine Learning.title: Possibility-based Inference: A Deterministic Framework for Robust and Reliable Uncertainty Quantification in Decision-Making
Machine Learning.summary: Decision-making under uncertainty remains a key issue in Machine Learning (ML), particularly in the deployment of safety-critical systems, where reliable quantification of system behavior is essential for evaluating behavioral impacts and strengthening confidence in ML models. This contribution, influenced by fuzzy set theory and grounded in Bayesian statistics, addresses challenges related to data precision and the performance-accuracy trade-off in Bayesian inference (BI). To this end, we introduce a possibility-based contrastive grade of prediction as an alternative quantification method to existing latent posterior-based approaches for parameter estimation (approximation) and model selection. Unlike conventional Bayesian inference, which represents uncertainty within the probabilistic framework, the proposed model adopts a possibility-based representation that allows uncertain and potentially conflicting information to be characterized more flexibly. Rather than focusing on isolated aspects of a problem, the resulting mathematical framework provides a systematic approach to data mining while mitigating overly confident, yet implausible predictions generated by highly specialized deep learning architectures.

Machine Learning.title: Decomposing Irregular Time Series into Interpretable Temporal Patterns with Mixture-of-Experts
Machine Learning.summary: Irregularly-spaced sequential data, such as transaction logs, encode multi-scale temporal structure that is critical for prediction but difficult to recover explicitly with standard sequence models, which often trade interpretability for performance. We introduce MoTIF, an interpretable framework using mixture-of-experts (MoE) attention to decompose irregular time series into temporal patterns spanning minute-to-year scales. Each expert is trained via temporal alignment that induces attention specialization to a designated cyclical or within-range pattern, with label-free routing supervision that learns to activate the correct expert from patterns present in the data. On synthetic data with known temporal structure, MoTIF recovers correct routing well above chance (0.389/0.829 for range/cyclical patterns vs. 0.091 random) and outperforms all baselines, including a standard transformer and an unspecialized MoE, on next-value prediction. On a public credit card transaction dataset, MoTIF achieves higher macro-F1 than all baselines for next-amount prediction. Its learned routing reveals structure a black-box model cannot: transactions are governed primarily by intraday and short-interval rhythms, while fraudulent transactions show bursty, calendar-agnostic timing versus the steadier periodicity of legitimate ones. On downstream fraud detection, MoTIF matches standard transformer and MoE baselines and clearly outperforms recent sequential recommendation models used as embedding baselines. These results show that decomposing temporal structure into interpretable, expert-specific patterns need not sacrifice predictive accuracy, offering a practical route to sequence models that are both accurate and auditable in high-stakes settings. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MoTIF-82E4.

Machine Learning.title: OpenSR-SRGAN: A Flexible Super-Resolution Framework for Multispectral Earth Observation Data
Machine Learning.summary:
Satellite images often contain useful measurements beyond visible red, green and blue light, but at a spatial resolution that is too coarse for some applications. Super-resolution methods estimate a finer-resolution image from these coarse observations. OpenSR-SRGAN is a modular, configuration-driven framework for training and benchmarking such models on multispectral Earth-observation data. The software enables users to train and evaluate configurable generator-discriminator architectures on arbitrary sensor band setups using concise YAML configurations, without modifying model code. All components, such as generators, discriminators, loss functions, training schedules, normalizations, and stability heuristics, are exposed through a common YAML interface. OpenSR-SRGAN makes it straightforward to reproduce experiments, compare architectures, and deploy super-resolution pipelines across diverse remote-sensing datasets.
  OpenSR-SRGAN supports complete end-to-end workflows with minimal setup: selecting architectures, scaling factors, band combinations, and training strategies entirely from configuration files. Although designed for remote-sensing super-resolution, its tensor-based model components can be adapted to other paired imaging data when suitable preprocessing and validation are provided.
Machine Learning.comment: Revised version corresponding to the published JOSS article

Machine Learning.title: C3: Speech-Guided KV Retrieval for Long-Context SpeechLLM Inference
Machine Learning.summary: Speech language models encode audio at a much higher rate than text, causing the KV cache to dominate the memory, bandwidth, and decoding cost of long-form generation. KV retrieval can reduce per-step access by attending to only a query-dependent subset of the cache, but existing methods are designed primarily for text and do not account for the structure of audio attention. We first show that retrieval errors may compound autoregressively into generation drift. We then analyze full audio attention during long-form generation and identify three properties relevant to retrieval: unequal attention concentration across query heads, non-contiguous audio support, and temporal continuity across decoding steps. Guided by these observations, we propose $C^3$(Cluster-Compete-Compete), which organizes audio KVs in a hierarchical key-space index, lets query heads sharing a KV head compete for a common retrieval budget, and adaptively reallocates retrieval resolution through paired split-merge updates. Across long-form speech recognition, translation, and summarization on four SpeechLLMs, $C^3$ achieves the strongest overall performance among retrieval methods under comparable final-KV access budgets, with particularly large gains in the tight-budget regime, while improving long-context decoding efficiency and accelerator-memory scaling.

Machine Learning.title: ScenicProver: A Framework for Compositional Probabilistic Verification of Learning-Enabled Systems
Machine Learning.summary: Full verification of learning-enabled cyber-physical systems (CPS) has long been intractable due to challenges including black-box components and complex real-world environments. Existing tools either provide formal guarantees for limited types of systems or test the system as a monolith, but no general framework exists for compositional analysis of learning-enabled CPS using varied verification techniques over complex real-world environments. This paper introduces a tool, ScenicProver, that aims to fill this gap by enabling the construction of sound, formally-checked assurance cases for CPS. ScenicProver is backed by a formal theory, which we lay out in this paper. ScenicProver supports: (1) environment modeling using the Scenic probabilistic programming language; (2) compositional system modeling with clear component interfaces, ranging from interpretable code to black boxes; (3) assume-guarantee contracts over those components using an extension of Linear Temporal Logic containing arbitrary Scenic expressions; (4) evidence generation through testing, formal proofs in Lean 4, and external assumptions; (5) sound combination of generated evidence using contract operators with Pacti; and (6) automatic generation of assurance cases tracking the provenance of system-level guarantees. We demonstrate its effectiveness through two case studies: one on an automatic emergency braking system with sensor fusion and one on drone safety. By leveraging manufacturer guarantees for sensors and focusing testing effort on uncertain conditions, our approach enables stronger probabilistic guarantees than monolithic testing with the same computational budget.
Machine Learning.comment: 36 pages, 8 figures. Full version (including appendices) of a paper submitted to TACAS 2027

Machine Learning.title: Causal Attention on CPU: A Cache-Aware and Load-Balanced Scheduling Kernel for Prefill
Machine Learning.summary: Agentic AI drives significant productivity gains across diverse domains, but concurrent long-context prefills from multiple agents can saturate GPU compute resources. Although CPUs offer a viable alternative, existing CPU attention kernels fall short in adapting to multi-tier cache hierarchies and lack effective thread scheduling. To address this, we introduce CACPU, a high-performance attention kernel featuring tiered cache blocking and an in-kernel task dispatching mechanism designed for causal full-sequence prefilling. CACPU achieves up to a 2.01x speedup over PyTorch SDPA, FlexAttention, and SGLang attention kernels. Integrated into SGLang, it reduces Time to First Token (TTFT) of Llama-3.1-8B by up to 1.74x while preserving model accuracy.

Machine Learning.title: Stochastic optimization methods through statistical whitening
Machine Learning.summary: We provide new statistical insights into designing stochastic optimization methods. By modeling the gradient via a normal distribution, we argue that the stochastic gradient should be whitened using its covariance. We give an online method for estimating the mean and variance of the gradients based on regularized likelihood or, equivalently, through a maximum a posteriori estimate. We then show how to use structured approximations to the covariance within this same framework, which includes diagonal and Kronecker-factored approximations. The diagonal approximation results in a method that is very closely related to Adam and performs as well in practice. The Kronecker approximation results in the new MN method, which is a variant of Shampoo and KL-Shampoo. We also recover Muon by applying this same statistical framework to the gradient direction rather than the full gradient. By combining this with a whitening step, we arrive at MN-Muon, a novel preconditioned version of Muon. Our experiments on GPT-2-type models at Chinchilla scale indicate that MND, the diagonal implementation of MN, outperforms both the Distributed Shampoo and the KL-Shampoo implementations in terms of stability, final validation loss and time taken. MND-Muon, the diagonal implementation of MN-Muon, improves on Muon in 21 of 24 paired GPT-small runs and achieves a lower best validation loss on GPT-medium, where it remains stable over the six tested learning rates. However, we found that NorMuon was comparable to MND-Muon and achieved a slightly lower validation loss on GPT-medium and at GPT-small batch 512 on FineWeb.

Machine Learning.title: Cyber-physical attack detection approaches in the wide-area measurement system
Machine Learning.summary: Improving situational awareness within the Smart Grid is an effective preventive measure to detect potential anomalies, and avoid their adverse consequences. A wide area measurement system (WAMS) based Phasor Measurement Unit (PMU) can assist in improving visibility within the grid by collecting relevant measurements including magnitude, phase angle, frequency, voltage, and current, with a precise GPS-based timestamp. So far, there are more than 2500 PMUs deployed in the North American power grid, where each of which generates between 30 and 60 samples/s, roughly 1.5 TB/month of streamed data. Thus, processing such large PMU streams requires expensive computational resources and faster algorithms. This paper provides state-of-the-art cyber and physical anomalies in the WAMS and analyses their impact on the integrity and availability of the system. Next, it investigates the current anomaly detection approach in historical and streaming PMU data, including conventional machine learning and hybrid approaches, and assesses their advantages and main drawbacks. Lastly, it sheds light on the importance of handling missing PMU data and concept drifts.

Machine Learning.title: RaMMOBO: Random Max-Margin Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization
Machine Learning.summary: Multi-objective Bayesian optimization (MOBO) maximizes $M$ expensive black-box objectives with the goal of approximating the Pareto set, whose objective vectors cannot be improved in one component without sacrificing another. A common quality measure is hypervolume, the volume in objective space dominated by these vectors relative to a reference point. Expected hypervolume improvement (EHVI) directly targets this metric and is one-step Bayes-optimal, but its standard computation scales exponentially with $M$, making it prohibitively expensive for many-objective problems. We introduce random max-margin multi-objective Bayesian optimization (RaMMOBO), whose acquisition function lower-bounds EHVI while requiring only linear cost in $M$ to evaluate. RaMMOBO measures the volume of a max-margin box contained in a candidate's hypervolume-improvement region and averages over random reweightings of the objective space, yielding a utility that is strictly Pareto-monotone on hypervolume-improving outcomes. It naturally handles noisy observations and different probabilistic surrogates and supports efficient gradient-based optimization. Across synthetic and real-world benchmarks, RaMMOBO matches or outperforms state-of-the-art methods, with largest gains at higher $M$, with acquisition optimization up to two orders of magnitude faster than qLogNEHVI. Our implementation is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/rammobo.

Machine Learning.title: Dynamic Quadtree Tokenization and Transformer for Adaptive Mesh PDE Forecasting
Machine Learning.summary: The quadratic attention cost of Vision Transformers (ViTs) forces a trade-off between spatial resolution and rollout horizon, particularly for fine-scale PDEs where shocks, reaction fronts, and material interfaces occupy small, evolving regions of the domain. Conventional neural surrogates also lack mechanisms to adapt resolution dynamically. We propose WAMRViT, a ViT that tokenizes inputs as balanced quadtrees using a wavelet-inspired refinement criterion, jointly encodes position and refinement level with 3D rotary positional embeddings, and regrids in cell space during inference for stable long-horizon rollouts. A multi-scale variant retains each leaf at its native source resolution and lets the model learn across resolution levels. Unlike fixed-budget adaptive-tokenization methods, WAMRViT imposes no predetermined token count and supports fully adaptive topology throughout autoregressive rollout. To our knowledge, it is the first machine-learning surrogate to natively tokenize multi-level Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) data. On uniform-grid benchmarks, uniform-patch WAMRViT improves finest-level region-of-interest VRMSE over a finest-patch uniform ViT while using substantially fewer tokens. The multi-scale variant achieves the lowest first-step full-field RMSE and VRMSE on both benchmarks and improves rollout-averaged full-field and refined-region accuracy at long horizons. With parallelized regridding, its end-to-end rollout cost lies between finest-patch and approximately token-matched coarser-patch ViTs. On a complex AMR combustion problem whose finest features cannot be represented natively by the evaluated uniform-grid baselines, WAMRViT operates on adaptive cells built from the simulator hierarchy and substantially reduces finest-level error at matched transformer capacity. Code: https://github.com/tonyzyl/wamrvit

Machine Learning.title: The Rise of Low Precision Floating Point
Machine Learning.summary: Floating point computing has dominated scientific computations since the 1950s because of its versatile ability to approximate real numbers with both sufficiently high precision and sufficiently great range. Since 1985, two specific formats have become standard across the industry, one with 32 bits which is adequate for many purposes and one with 64 bits which allows numbers with both much higher precision and much greater range for applications where these are needed. However, during the past decade, deep learning has come to dominate computation, and narrower floating point formats with lower precision and reduced range have steadily become more common. In this article we discuss this phenomenon, why it is happening, how various 16-bit, 8-bit and even 4-bit floating point formats have been developed, and efforts to standardize these formats.

Machine Learning.title: A Framework for Task-Agnostic Counterfactual Fairness in Transformers through Activation Steering
Machine Learning.summary: Bias in transformer-based models is a growing concern as these architectures become more prevalent in automated decision-making systems, such as prediction models for hiring, lending, and clinical treatment recommendation. Mechanistic interpretability (MI) is a growing body of work that measures meaningful causal effects of activations on model output by identifying human-interpretable features encoded in model activations. When such features correspond to sensitive attributes, they provide a direct way to quantify the bias those attributes introduce and to causally intervene to mitigate it. However, counterfactual fairness (CF) methods have not been systematically adapted to this setting of intervening on interpretable mechanisms in transformers. We propose a framework, Mechanistic Interpretability for Counterfactual Fairness (MICF), that utilizes MI tools to reformulate CF constraints in terms of transformer activations, unifying former approaches into a single pipeline for fairness analysis in transformers. MICF does not require a prior causal model or specific transformer architecture. We evaluate MICF on real-world tabular data and show that CF can be improved across different prediction tasks.

Machine Learning.title: Para-Gaussian Approximations of Random Deep Neural Networks
Machine Learning.summary: It is known that randomly initialized neural networks have Gaussian behaviour in the $n\to \infty$ limit. Unfortunately, this approximation can be poor for finite $n$ and gets worse as one goes deeper into the network. In this work, we develop a more accurate approximation that is \emph{slightly} non-Gaussian, which we call the para-Gaussian distribution and is constructed from the Hermite polynomials. We show how this para-Gaussian approximation can lead to a practical recursive method to approximate the deeper layers of the network. Finally, we apply this theory to linear neural networks (where things can be solved exactly) and to ReLU neural networks (where things can be approximated).

Machine Learning.title: Understanding ID-Text Complementarity in Sequential Recommendation
Machine Learning.summary: Dense retrieval-based Sequential Recommendation (SR) systems increasingly leverage text features to represent items, and generally do so in one of two ways: (i) by completely replacing ID embeddings with text embeddings, or (ii) by carefully combining ID and text embeddings through complex fusion mechanisms. While these lines of work have produced strong recommendation performances, they offer conflicting perspectives on ID-text complementarity, or the extent to which ID and text embeddings specialize in modeling different signals: the former suggests a lack of complementarity, and the latter argues it exists but must be harnessed carefully. Moreover, neither workstream conducts an in-depth study of ID-text complementarity. We aim to clarify this picture by developing a rigorous understanding of the complementarity of ID- and text-based SR models in this work. Our study reveals that these models do learn complementary signals, meaning that either should provide performance gain when used properly alongside the other. Motivated by this, we introduce and evaluate a new, simple SR baseline that preserves ID-text complementarity through independent model training, then harnesses it via ensembling. Despite this method's simplicity, we show it outperforms several competitive SR baselines, implying a third perspective on ID-text complementarity: both features are necessary to achieve state-of-the-art SR performance, but complex fusion strategies are not.

Machine Learning.title: Generalized Intention Modeling in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
Machine Learning.summary: Modeling an opponent's intent is critical for effective decision-making in non-cooperative, competitive, and general-sum multi-agent reinforcement learning. Existing opponent modeling methods encode intent using an embedding derived from episode information chosen a priori, such as the opponent's next action or a future environment state, and use this to guide the ego-agent's behavior. These approaches assume that the chosen information is universally representative of intent; however, we show empirically that this is not the case as intentions are often task- and environment-dependent. To address this, we introduce a task-adaptive opponent modeling framework that learns a performance-driven mixture of multiple intent representations. We further introduce a new intention representation that maximizes mutual information with the ego-agent's future returns, thereby capturing opponent information that is most directly relevant to performance. Our approach consistently matches or exceeds the performance of state-of-the-art baselines across diverse tasks and yields insights into when and why different opponent modeling strategies succeed.

Machine Learning.title: Quantization of Large Models with Weight Outliers and Sparsity
Machine Learning.summary: Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces the memory burden of large model deployment by casting the high precision trained weights to fewer bits. While this promotes memory-efficient inference, it also incurs quantization error that impairs model performance. To compensate for quantization error, the present contribution decomposes the original trained weights into a quantized matrix, a low-rank component, and a sparse matrix that accounts for outlier rows in the weights. Due to analytical intractability and the discrete structure of the decomposition, a simulated annealing search is employed to explore candidate decompositions while avoiding poor local minima. Numerical tests demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach across a broad suite of large language models, including Llama 3.2 1B, Llama 3.2 3B, Llama 3.1 8B, and Qwen2.5 7B, evaluated on natural language generation benchmarks using 4-bit NF4 and FP4 quantizers. The novel method can markedly outperform direct quantization while incurring minimal memory overhead.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on On-Device Intelligence: Foundation Models under Real-World Constraints

Machine Learning.title: OCELOT: Planetary-Scale Species Distribution Modeling with Satellite Foundation Embeddings
Machine Learning.summary: Large-scale repositories of species observations now contain billions of occurrence records from around the world, but these sightings cluster heavily in human-accessible areas. Existing models use only a small fraction of these records and are not evaluated on extrapolating to remote, unvisited regions--where species distribution models can be used as geographic priors to help classify data from camera traps and acoustic recorders. We scale relative occurrence species distribution models by training a multimodal implicit neural representation network called OCELOT that fuses spatial coordinates with satellite foundation embeddings on two orders of magnitude more observations than previous work: 2 billion GBIF records across 100,000 taxa. Scaling to this regime requires co-designing the data pipeline, taxonomic representation, loss formulation, and model architecture: spatiotemporal thinning and sub-linear cell sampling correct for spatial redundancy and observer bias, while an additive taxonomic readout shares representations across species, genera, and families to improve predictions for rare taxa. To evaluate performance in remote areas, we benchmark geographic extrapolation using the NDCG metric on spatial block holdouts up to 600 km. Satellite foundation embeddings improve extrapolation by 51% over coordinate-only models and outperform classical bioclimatic rasters. The resulting model also matches or outperforms existing baselines on established interpolation benchmarks, demonstrating that optimizing for geographic extrapolation does not compromise in-distribution accuracy.

Machine Learning.title: DELBERT-2: Pretrained Fingerprint Language Models for DEL Protein Binder Prediction
Machine Learning.summary: We present DELBERT-2, a pretrained fingerprint language model that converts sparse molecular fingerprints into unified token sequences using a ModernBERT encoder trained with masked language modelling on 2.5M molecules from the AIRCHECK DEL corpus. We evaluate across six targets (WDR91, WDR12, SETDB1, PLCZ1, LRRK2, DCAF7) under three out-of-distribution (OOD) protocols: hierarchical cluster splits probe chemical novelty, library splits test cross-library transfer, and building-block splits assess compositional generalization. DELBERT-2 consistently improves PR-AUC and NDCG@1000 relative to LightGBM ensemble baselines and transformers trained from scratch, with the largest gains in stringent OOD regimes. DELBERT-2 achieves 13.28+/-3.72 enrichment factor at top-100 vs. 12.36+/-3.75 for no-pretraining (p=0.040), representing 7.4% improvement and 13x enrichment over random selection. These results demonstrate that fingerprint-centric self-supervised learning effectively improves hit prioritization under distribution shift, enabling practical DEL virtual screening. Code is available at \hyperlink{https://github.com/GenerativeDrugDiscovery/DELBERT-2}{DELBERT-2}.
Machine Learning.comment: 14 pages, 6 figures, 2026 Workshop on Generative and Agentic AI for Biology (ICML 2026)

Machine Learning.title: Automated grounding verification of AI statements about chest radiographs
Machine Learning.summary: A grounding verifier checks a statement about a patient's image against the radiology report and the cited evidence. The state-of-the-art methods for testing these verifiers remove or replace the cited evidence while the patient's report stays unchanged. To our knowledge, no existing method checks both the report and the cited evidence. We present Building Report And Citation Examples (BRACE), an automated framework that builds training examples from public radiology reports and Radiopaedia articles. We compared a lexical baseline and 42 verifiers with 0.1-284B parameters on 5 different public chest radiograph datasets. At a threshold accepting 0.90 of the supported test examples, verifiers trained with BRACE accepted a mean of only 0.239 of AI-written statements contradicted by the report. Verifiers trained without contradicted examples passed the state-of-the-art tests, yet accepted most of these statements (0.830 on average). With citations retrieved from held-out Radiopaedia articles, verifiers trained with BRACE accepted 0.169 of AI-written statements with an agreeing report and an unsupporting citation. By contrast, zero-shot large language models mostly checked the report and not the citation (they accepted 0.830 of these statements). We further assessed the framework manually, with two board-certified radiologists independently labeling a sample of test reports. The framework's labels agreed with each radiologist (k > 0.910) almost as closely as the radiologists agreed with each other (k = 0.952). Moreover, instantiating the framework for food allergens in recipes, we showed that it extends beyond clinical applications. A verifier built the same way accepted 0.493 of the statements contradicted by the recipe, whereas a lexical baseline accepted 0.898. Using both the report and the cited evidence, verifiers trained with BRACE could check AI statements before clinicians read them.

Machine Learning.title: D-MOD: Diffusion mode estimation for accelerated MRI
Machine Learning.summary: Diffusion models are powerful priors for accelerated MRI reconstruction, but most current methods are posterior samplers, which return a random draw from the posterior. A reproducible and high-quality reconstruction often requires averaging many samples, resulting in a high computational cost. We introduce D-MOD, a fast algorithm that instead provides a posterior mode. It uses a minorize-maximize algorithm on a lower bound of the smoothed log-posterior, which provably increases the objective. Each iteration draws S noisy samples of the current estimate at the current noise level, denoises them with a pretrained diffusion model, and combines their average with the measured k-space through a conjugate-gradient (CG) solve. We anneal the noise levels, as the distance between the bound and its target decays quadratically with noise. On fastMRI brain (T1, T2, FLAIR), a single D-MOD reconstruction exceeds, in PSNR, the 10-sample finite-MMSE estimates of DPS, DAPS and SNORE-P and stays within 0.31 dB of the strongest baselines (DiffPIR, DDS). This approach thus provides a fast deterministic reconstruction algorithm (11-73 times faster than MMSE estimates), which is useful in a clinical setting.

Machine Learning.title: Outstrumental Variable Regression
Machine Learning.summary: Estimating the causal effect of a treatment $X$ on an outcome $Y$ from observational data in the presence of unobserved confounding requires additional structure or assumptions. Existing identification strategies such as instrumental variable regression exploit exogenous variation in only the treatment. We show that the causal effect can also be identified if the outcome mechanism varies across a finite set of environments, even if the treatment distribution is unchanged. Concretely, we introduce Outstrumental Variable Regression (OVR), which proceeds in three steps: (i) compute the conditional expectation of $Y$ given $X$ in each environment; (ii) form the vector of differences in these conditional expectations between all environments and a reference environment (we call this vector contrast); and (iii) regress $Y$ on $X$ while adjusting for the contrast and environment. We prove that this yields the true causal effect if the following two conditions hold: inclusion restriction, i.e., the contrast determines the conditional confounding bias; and positivity, i.e., the treatment varies sufficiently strongly after adjustment. We prove that a finite-sample version of OVR is consistent under regularity conditions and demonstrate the procedure's effectiveness on synthetic and real-world data.

Machine Learning.title: KINDER: Kernel-based Independence for Fair Representation Learning via Prototype-space Erasure
Machine Learning.summary: Concept erasure is a prominent approach to achieving fairness in machine learning through the removal of sensitive attributes from learned representations. Prior concept erasure methods typically define debiasing indirectly through the failure of a chosen adversary, probe, or fairness penalty, which makes the target of erasure dependent on a particular decoder family or optimization setup. We introduce KINDER, which directly removes sensitive-attribute information from intermediate representations with respect to a chosen family of prototype functionals, and is compatible with any deep model containing an intermediate feature space, independent of the architecture, task type, or training paradigm. KINDER operates in a random Fourier feature space, where it estimates a sensitive subspace from protected group prototypes and projects representations onto its orthogonal complement. Thus, it forms an explicit representation cleaning mechanism distinct from prior fairness control studies. We conduct extensive experiments across diverse settings and show the effectiveness of KINDER on (i) supervised and self-supervised settings, (ii) classification, regression, and image segmentation tasks, and (iii) diverse data modalities, including visual, textual, and tabular data. Code and trained models are available at: https://github.com/abtinmU/KINDER

Machine Learning.title: Model Collapse Is Avoidable Even as Real Data Vanishes: A Sharp Criterion for Iterative Gaussian Estimation
Machine Learning.summary: Large generative models are commonly trained on data collected from the open web, which may contain data produced by previous generations of the same model. Previous work has shown that recursively training on model-generated data can progressively degrade model performance, a phenomenon known as model collapse. Yet, generative models continue to improve dramatically over time. Existing theory suggests that this is enabled by the availability of new real data at each iteration, kept separate from generated data. However, exact separation is not realistic, and uncurated data is still commonly used. We bridge this gap by considering a more realistic setup in which real and generated data are not handled differently during training. Specifically, we present a comprehensive theoretical study of iterative estimation of the mean and covariance of a multivariate Gaussian distribution. At each iteration, samples are drawn from a mixture of the real data distribution and the estimated distribution from the previous iteration, but are used indistinguishably. We provide a single equivalent condition for consistency of the mean and covariance estimators in Euclidean norms, and convergence to zero of the expected squared 2-Wasserstein distance between the estimated and true distributions. Using this result, we show that consistency holds, i.e., model collapse is avoided, for any fixed real data fraction above zero, and even for a fraction that vanishes across iterations, provided it does not vanish too quickly. However, more real data (or data curation) remains important at practical finite times: the convergence rate of the mean estimator deteriorates as the real data fraction approaches zero. We support our results with an empirical investigation of the theoretical setup, and with experiments on iterative training of a diffusion model on CIFAR-10 that correlate with our theory.

Machine Learning.title: Matryoshka Hash Representations for Model-Aware Compact Semantic Retrieval
Machine Learning.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) depends on dense retrieval: each document is stored as a learned vector, and queries are answered by nearest-neighbor search. Keeping one full-precision vector per document dominates index cost at corpus scale, so systems replace each vector with a short code of a few bytes (quantization). Standard quantizers such as product quantization (PQ) pick the code that best reconstructs the original vector, but reconstruction is only a proxy for retrieval: at a few bytes per document, a model-aware code trained on the retriever's ranking signal uses the budget better. A single code is even more useful if its short prefixes are each directly searchable, letting a deployment set its efficiency-quality operating point without re-encoding the corpus. But training all prefixes under one objective makes the early bits a compromise across budgets: short codes improve while the full-width code degrades. Binary codes sharpen the conflict, since a gradient step either flips a stored bit or leaves it unchanged. We introduce Matryoshka Hash Representations (MHR), a two-stage procedure that separates full-width training from prefix organization. MHR first learns a longer binary code, then freezes the model and trains zero-initialized residual code adaptors for directly searchable prefixes. Documents are stored at one bit per coordinate, queries keep continuous logits as in PQ, and search runs on FAISS FastScan. Trained on MS MARCO and zero-shot transferred to seven BEIR datasets, one MHR code reaches 0.502 NDCG@10 at 16 bytes and 0.556 at 32 bytes, against 0.404 and 0.524 for the best compact baselines; the gains hold across training seeds, on all 13 public BEIR datasets, and against off-the-shelf binary Matryoshka embeddings with stronger backbones. The same code also helps shortlist candidates for reranking and prune low-storage graph indexes such as LEANN.

Machine Learning.title: IsoAlign: Isoform-Aware DNA-Protein Alignment via Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures
Machine Learning.summary: Genomic foundation models (GFMs) have emerged as a powerful paradigm for learning DNA sequence representations, yet existing self-supervised pretraining strategies overlook alternative splicing and underperform compared to specialized models. To address this gap, we introduce IsoAlign, a multimodal framework that grounds genomic pretraining in isoform-aware DNA-protein alignment to learn biologically meaningful representations. IsoAlign aligns transcripts to their corresponding protein isoforms, capturing both coding sequences and broader regulatory contexts, using two Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPA): DNA-Protein JEPA (DP-JEPA), which predicts protein representations from DNA using contrastive alignment, and Isoform-Masked JEPA (IM-JEPA), which models relationships among alternative isoforms of the same gene through masked protein prediction. We evaluate the learned DNA representations of these architectures across a multi-metric evaluation suite spanning tasks, including the prediction of pathogenicity, fitness, gene expression, and TF binding. Our results demonstrate that isoform-aware cross-modal alignment using JEPA significantly improves functional representations and downstream performance, establishing a promising direction for GFM pretraining.

Machine Learning.title: Propagation of Chaos in Contextual Flow Maps
Machine Learning.summary: We develop a quantitative statistical theory of transformers in the large-context regime by adopting the abstraction of contextual flow maps (CFMs): dynamical systems that evolve a distinguished token in the presence of a contextual measure across a stack of attention blocks. Within this framework, the finite-context model approximates an idealized infinite-context system in which the contextual measure is replaced by its underlying population, so that the context length $n$ becomes a statistical resource. Exploiting the McKean--Vlasov structure of the dynamics and the classical machinery of propagation of chaos, we establish a forward bound controlling the deviation between the finite- and infinite-context CFMs uniformly along depth, and a backward bound controlling the deviation between the corresponding training trajectories uniformly across iterations of online gradient descent. Both bounds achieve the optimal Wasserstein rate $n^{-1/d}$ for general CFMs and parametric rate $n^{-1/2}$ for a restricted class of CFMs that includes transformers as a special case. The analysis rests on a new Eulerian adjoint formulation of the loss gradient and stability estimates for the resulting forward--adjoint system, both of which may be of independent interest.

Machine Learning.title: Effector: A Python Package for Global and Regional Feature Effects
Machine Learning.summary: Effector is a Python package for interpreting machine learning (ML) models that are trained on tabular data through global and regional feature effects. Global effects, like Partial Dependence Plot (PDP) and Accumulated Local Effects (ALE), are widely used for explaining tabular ML models due to their simplicity -- each feature's average influence on the prediction is summarized by a single 1D plot. However, when features are interacting, global effects can be misleading. Regional effects address this by partitioning the input space into disjoint subregions with minimal interactions within each and computing a separate regional effect per subspace. Regional effects are then visualized by a set of 1D plots per feature. Effector provides efficient implementations of state-of-the-art global and regional feature effects methods under a unified API. The package integrates seamlessly with major ML libraries like scikit-learn and PyTorch. It is designed to be modular and extensible, and comes with comprehensive documentation and tutorials. Effector is an open-source project publicly available on Github at https://github.com/givasile/effector.

Machine Learning.title: WaiT for the Signal: Simple Frequency-Aware Flow-Matching
Machine Learning.summary: As image generation models scale to ever higher resolutions, global coherence, local detail, and texture fidelity become critical axes for generation quality. However, standard flow matching treats all spatial frequencies uniformly, ignoring the natural frequency hierarchy where high-frequency bands become indistinguishable from pure noise far earlier than coarse structures. We introduce WaiT, a Wavelet-aware image Transformer that decomposes generation into coarse and fine bands via lossless wavelets. True to its name, the high-frequency bands wait for the signal: staying pure noise until coarse structure has emerged, then joining the flow for joint refinement. Since standard FID discards fine-grained detail through aggressive downsampling, we introduce a more stringent three-axis evaluation protocol to assess quality at native resolution. On ImageNet 512x512, WaiT achieves a pixel-space FID of 1.43 and is Pareto-optimal across all three axes, reducing sampling compute by up to 50%. With our largest 2B model, we set a new state-of-the-art FID of 1.3 for pixel-space models on ImageNet 512 resolution. Our formulation outperforms even the strongest latent-space models on texture fidelity, and scales seamlessly to high-resolution OpenImages and to video generation, achieving a state-of-the-art FVD of 0.84 on Kinetics-600 with no algorithmic modifications.

Machine Learning.title: ProLand: A New Infeasible Manifold Optimization Method for LoRA Fine-Tuning
Machine Learning.summary: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) enables parameter-efficient fine-tuning but can suffer from redundant basis directions. Constraining the basis factor to the Stiefel manifold addresses this redundancy through orthonormality. Landing methods allow temporarily infeasible iterates to explore a neighborhood of the manifold while progressively restoring orthogonality without per-step retractions. To improve optimization efficiency while retaining this flexibility, we introduce ProLand (Product-space Landing), a retraction-free optimizer that combines coordinated factor updates with Muon-style spectral directions. By designing the updates in the space of the represented weight increment, ProLand separates objective optimization from orthogonality restoration, supporting efficient feasibility recovery. This coordinated construction also enables Muon-style directions to guide objective optimization while preserving that separation. Experiments cover four GLUE validation tasks on DeBERTa-v3-base and seven language benchmarks on Qwen2.5-3B, Llama-3.2-3B, and Moonlight-16B-A3B across multiple adapter ranks. Across these 11 tasks, ProLand achieves the highest average score among the compared methods in every tested encoder and decoder model-rank configuration.

Machine Learning.title: Localized anomaly detection with a calorimeter normalizing flow
Machine Learning.summary: Normalizing flows trained as fast calorimeter simulators also give the likelihood of each shower, which can serve as an anomaly score. Because this likelihood sums over every voxel, a signal confined to a few voxels can be lost in the fluctuations of the rest of the shower. For example, in a public benchmark dataset in which a long-lived neutral particle decays to two photons, the CaloFlow likelihood used in previous work selects less than 5% of the signal at a background efficiency of $10^{-3}$ when the particle has the largest simulated mass and decays at or just behind the front face of the calorimeter. In this work, we define a regional anomaly score by summing the squared latent coordinates of the same flow within small detector regions around the point where the particle enters the calorimeter, with the threshold set using background showers alone. At the same background efficiency, this regional anomaly score selects more than 95% of the signal. The per-coordinate likelihood terms, summed over the same regions, perform equally well, but the squared latent coordinates have a known distribution for background showers and clearly illustrate when a shower departs from it. Therefore, normalizing flows may be sensitive to new physics, even if the global likelihood is not.

Machine Learning.title: Advancing Open and Reproducible Relational Learning: RelArena-$α$, TabPFN-Rel and RPI
Machine Learning.summary:
This first release of Prior Labs in relational learning shows our continued commitment to open science. We open-source three pieces of software that we expect to accelerate research in the field towards meaningful real-world impact. We aim to steer further development based on feedback from, and in collaboration with, the community. Given the early stage of development, our $α$-release targets researchers and early-adopting practitioners. Over the past years, a variety of datasets and tasks for relational learning have emerged, but the community has not converged on a reliable, reproducible way to compare different methods on these tasks. Our $α$-release, RelArena-$α$, provides a unified framework for running and comparing baselines on RelBench v1 by standardizing data loading, evaluation protocols, tuning regimes, and support for systems with custom tuning, inspired by established tabular benchmarks such as TabArena. We plan to work with the research community to further develop RelArena-$α$ into a catalyst for progress in the relational learning community. We release the initial version of TabPFN-Rel, a purpose-built relational harness for TabPFN-3. Currently ranked first among models on RelArena-$α$, TabPFN-Rel makes key improvements upon RDBLearn. Beyond its ranking, TabPFN-Rel serves as a strong baseline, adding to the growing evidence that flattening a relational database into a single table remains competitive with specialized relational architectures on real-world tasks.
  To facilitate adoption of relational learning methods in research and industry, we release an initial $α$-version of our Relational Predictive Interface, RPI, an open-source, model-agnostic interface that enables early adopters to easily define problems on new databases and apply any model implemented in RelArena-$α$, including TabPFN-Rel, to these problems.

Machine Learning.title: Spectral and Conformal: Neural Network Methods for Calibrated Trajectory Prediction and Control-Point Intervals
Machine Learning.summary: Autonomous systems that navigate their environment need methods to quickly assess the feasibility and safety of desired trajectories. Traditional solutions that rely on numerical integration can be computationally heavy, while fast data-driven surrogates lack the formal guarantees that numerical approaches provide. This work demonstrates a framework that uses (1) a neural network with a spectral backbone to learn trajectories and quantile bands with built-in constraints (initial conditions and stability); (2) a modified conformal quantile regression to provide calibrated, joint trajectory-level coverage; and (3) interval arithmetic to extend noise-free coverage guarantees to control points. After refactoring the network for inference, the trajectory inference time for a quadrotor under a closed-loop linear quadratic regulator is 3.45~ms on a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W. The total pipeline time, including trajectory inference time, is 9.81~ms, or approximately 100~Hz, consistent with typical control rates.
Machine Learning.comment: 26 pages, 10 figures, 7 tables. Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research

Machine Learning.title: Consilience for Verifier-Free Test-Time Scaling
Machine Learning.summary:
Test-time scaling often uses an external verifier, such as compilers and test cases in coding or trained value functions in robotics applications, to obtain high-quality rollouts. Verifier-free test-time scaling (or VF-TTS) is gaining extensive attention as a mechanism to enhance Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning, primarily because we do not have access to such high-quality verifiers in many real-world applications. Among existing VF-TTS methods, confidence-based VF-TTS methods, which compute and rank rollouts solely by confidence, are particularly promising. Such methods introduce near-zero overhead for sample evaluation and require minimal access to internal model states, making the methods highly flexible across models and tasks.
  In this paper, we demonstrate a critical limitation of existing confidence-based VF-TTS methods by showing that such methods catastrophically break down on complex tasks. We observe a very interesting phenomenon: uniformly high confidence frequently indicates a failure to explore, favoring confidently wrong answers. To address this, our core insight is that robust cognitive search requires a specific confidence trajectory pattern: such methods perform exploratory branching at the beginning, as manifested by low initial confidence, and converge to a high final confidence solution. To implement this insight, we introduce consilience, a novel selection framework that explicitly evaluates the temporal asymmetry of confidence in reasoning. We operationalize this via a combinatorial metric that actively penalizes high initial confidence while strictly demanding final certainty. Extensive experiments covering both graduate-level mathematics problems and free-form code generation demonstrate that consilience effectively outperforms existing baselines, validating our novel perspective on completion confidence.

Machine Learning.title: OPINE: Orthogonal Projection in Invertible Nonlinear Embeddings for Turbulent Flows
Machine Learning.summary: Proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) represents physical fields with orthogonal modes ordered by variance, so that one decomposition gives reduced coordinates in every dimension, but it needs many modes when the data lie near a curved manifold. Nonlinear autoencoders are more compact, but their information loss happens inside a nonlinear encoder, and a model trained with one latent dimension gives no model with a smaller one. We introduce Orthogonal Projection in Invertible Nonlinear Embeddings (OPINE), which learns an invertible nonlinear change of coordinates and performs POD in the transformed coordinates. Because the map is invertible, all information loss occurs in the POD projection, and ordering its basis after training gives reduced coordinates of every smaller dimension from a single model. Training alternates gradient updates of the map with a damped update that tracks the evolving POD subspace, and we prove that this update converges locally to the exact POD subspace. We evaluate OPINE on synthetic manifolds, chaotic Kuramoto-Sivashinsky dynamics, forced Burgers turbulence, two-dimensional Kolmogorov flow, and three-dimensional minimal channel flow. OPINE is more accurate than POD at every tested retained dimension above one, and on the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky and Burgers dynamics, it is more accurate than convolutional and fully connected autoencoders by more than two orders of magnitude at the largest retained dimension.

Machine Learning.title: Rethinking Layer-wise Model Merging through Chain of Merges
Machine Learning.summary: Model merging has emerged as a simple yet effective method to fuse models without re-training. Existing techniques operate at the level of individual layers, thereby overlooking the inter-layer dependencies inherent in deep networks. We show that this simplification induces distributional mismatches in intermediate activations during merging, as changes applied to early layers fail to propagate to downstream ones. We identify these mismatches as a form of covariate shift that compounds across the network. To address this issue, we propose Chain of Merges (CoM), a novel procedure that sequentially merges weights across layers while accounting for inter-layer interactions. In particular, CoM mitigates covariate shift through a series of regression problems, where input activations are recomputed at each step to reflect the updated representations. Additionally, we introduce a dynamic weighting mechanism that prioritizes task-layer pairs most susceptible to performance degradation, improving robustness during merging. Experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate that CoM achieves state-of-the-art performance across heterogeneous tasks.

Machine Learning.title: The Hardness of Estimating Cross-Entropy Risk for Language Models
Machine Learning.summary: Language models, once pretrained, are routinely assessed by the holdout method, which estimates their per-token cross-entropy risk---a quantity that may be finite or infinite. We prove possibility and impossibility theorems that characterize the hardness of this estimation problem. The estimand depends on two objects: the unknown data distribution $p$ and the distribution $q$ induced by the language model under study. Our ignorance of $p$ is empirical, whereas our ignorance of $q$, or at least of its tail, is mathematical; so the parameter space {\em should} range over pairs $(p,q)$---a product space---to fully capture our ignorance. {\em Negative results}: no estimator is pointwise consistent, even when the parameter space is restricted to full-support models and to data distributions whose expected text length is below a fixed bound; worse, every estimator fails on a dense set of pairs. {\em Positive results}: the holdout estimator becomes pointwise consistent when the models are further restricted to Transformers or, architecture-neutrally, to full-support models with a finite context window; and, where no such design is in place, it still consistently estimates the risk capped at any fixed threshold, which suffices for screening candidate models in practice. {\em Lesson}: designs such as the Transformer architecture and finite context windows, although adopted for computational or engineering reasons, pay a {\em statistical dividend}: they suffice to make pointwise consistency possible---a dividend visible only in how they turn a negative result into positive ones.
Machine Learning.comment: Substantially revised and expanded version under a new title. Retains the main impossibility results of v1 and adds a new positive theorem concerning Transformers, which prompted a thorough overhaul of the paper's motivation, organization, and discussion of its significance

Machine Learning.title: Curriculum Learning for Safety Alignment
Machine Learning.summary: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is a widely used approach for safety alignment that aims to reduce harmful behaviors in large language models. However, prior work shows that it can be brittle and exhibits poor out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization. In this paper we investigate whether Curriculum Learning can improve the robustness of DPO-based safety alignment. We propose Staged-Competence, a curriculum-based framework that organizes preference data by difficulty, employs competence-based sampling, and progressively updates the reference model during training. Averaged across three model families and three training seeds, Staged-Competence reduces OOD harmful response rates by 13.6 percentage points and attack success rates across five jailbreak attacks by 16.5 percentage points, while preserving general capabilities and maintaining near-zero over-refusal. We further show that Staged-Competence: (1) matches baseline safety performance with only 75% of the training data, demonstrating improved data efficiency and (2) yields better separation between safe and unsafe responses. Staged-Competence is agnostic to the underlying policy optimization loss and can extend to other DPO variants and alignment domains beyond safety. Additionally, we find multiple inconsistencies in standard RLHF datasets and create a cleaner combined version, named PiKacHHU. Our code is available at https://github.com/Sandeep5500/curriculum-learning-for-safety and the dataset at https://huggingface.co/datasets/etrigan5500/PiKacHHU.

Machine Learning.title: Black-Box Combinatorial Optimization with Order-Invariant Reinforcement Learning
Machine Learning.summary: We introduce an order-invariant reinforcement learning framework for black-box combinatorial optimization. Classical estimation-of-distribution algorithms (EDAs) often rely on learning explicit variable dependency graphs, which can be costly and fail to capture complex interactions efficiently. In contrast, we parameterize a multivariate autoregressive generative model trained without a fixed variable ordering. By sampling random generation orders during training, a form of information-preserving dropout, the model is encouraged to be invariant to variable order, promoting search-space diversity, and shaping the model to focus on the most relevant variable dependencies, improving sample efficiency. We adapt Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to this setting, providing stable policy-gradient updates from scale-invariant advantages. Across a wide range of benchmark algorithms and problem instances of varying sizes, our method frequently achieves the best performance and consistently avoids catastrophic failures.

Machine Learning.title: Do Personal Adapters Carry Over Across Sessions? Separating Personal From Population Gains When Calibrating EEG Foundation Models for Motor Imagery
Machine Learning.summary: Every new user of a motor imagery brain-computer interface must be calibrated, and users typically return on different days. A common approach with electroencephalography (EEG) foundation models fits a small personal adapter on a frozen backbone, but evaluations are usually confined to one session and rarely separate the user's own contribution from that of the population model. We quantified personal adapters with two paired contrasts, the net gain of a user's own adapter over the population model and its advantage over adapters fitted to other users, for three frozen foundation models (CBraMod, REVE and LaBraM). In 235 held-out subjects from three datasets, same-session calibration produced a positive net gain in all nine model and dataset combinations (means of 1.5 to 5.4 percentage points), and the gain remained positive when population training was quadrupled. In 54 two-session subjects, adapters fitted on the first day still improved on the population model on the second day by 1.31 points for REVE and 1.64 points for LaBraM (Holm-adjusted p<0.01), retaining 61% and 83% of the gain from same-day recalibration, whereas the gain for CBraMod was 0.04 points and indistinguishable from zero. Same-day recalibration gave the highest mean accuracy for all three models, and adding 5 to 20 second-day labels to the first-day adapter mostly fell short of it. Whether personal adapters carry over across sessions therefore depends on the model and must be tested per model, and personalization should be reported against both a population reference and exchanged parameters, including across sessions.
Machine Learning.comment: 8 pages main text + 9 pages supplementary material (appended). v2: substantially revised and retitled; adds cross-session experiments for CBraMod, REVE and LaBraM, classical baselines and an analysis of population-training strength. Code and results: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23807847

Machine Learning.title: CAPER: Circuit-Aware Parameter-Efficient Reasoning in LLMs for Analog Verification
Machine Learning.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate analog circuits, yet every netlist must also be verified. We propose LLMs as verification assistants for analog circuits that flag unmet specifications and reliability issues that appear under process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) variation. These issues emerge from how circuit stages combine, a structure that generic parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods such as LoRA do not capture. To this end, we introduce CAPER, a circuit-aware PEFT method that adds a small branch alongside LoRA to read each stage's properties from the LLM and combine them from the relevant stages. In deciding whether a feedback loop is negative, LoRA and a high-rank adapter stay at chance, whereas CAPER answers every test case correctly. For comparator latches, where 11 of 90 LLM-written designs that work under nominal conditions fail under PVT variation, CAPER likewise learns to flag such latent failures, while generic adapters stay near chance. These results show that adding circuit knowledge to PEFT makes such analog verification checks learnable through fine-tuning.
Machine Learning.comment: Presented at IBM IEEE CAS/EDS - AI Compute Symposium (AICS) 2026 held at IBM, Yorktown Heights, NY, USA, on 28th October
