This narrows the gap between training and validation performance and improves reliability on unseen data, as evident from the experiments.
  Although superficially similar to DropConnect, PerNodeDrop operates at the sample level. It drops weights at the sample level, not the batch level. An expected-loss analysis formalizes how its perturbations attenuate excessive co-adaptation while retaining predictive interactions. Empirical evaluations on vision, text, and audio benchmarks indicate improved generalization relative to the standard noise-based regularizer.

Machine Learning.title: Spatial-Temporal Learning-Based Distributed Routing for Dynamic LEO Satellite Networks
Machine Learning.summary: This paper proposes a spatial-temporal learning-based routing framework for dynamic low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite networks. The routing problem is formulated as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP), where each satellite independently selects its next hop using network-state observations and destination information. A graph attention network (GAT) extracts spatial features from the dynamic satellite topology and queue states, while a long short-term memory (LSTM) network captures their temporal evolution. The resulting representation is integrated into a deep Q-network (DQN) for destination-aware next-hop selection without a separate traffic-prediction stage. Simulations in a 45-satellite LEO constellation under normal and bursty traffic demonstrate packet delivery performance comparable to a graph neural network (GNN)-enhanced routing baseline, although the proposed method incurs higher delay and queue occupancy. Ablation studies further demonstrate the complementary benefits of spatial and temporal learning.
Machine Learning.comment: 6 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to the IEEE International Conference on Communications (ICC) 2027

Machine Learning.title: Lower Bounds for Stochastic First-Order Algorithms with Variance Reduction in Nonconvex--Concave Minimax Optimization
Machine Learning.summary: We establish complexity lower bounds for stochastic first-order algorithms in nonconvex--concave minimax optimization, allowing algorithms to use variance reduction. Our main contribution is a lower bound for a zero-respecting algorithm class that permits variance reduction, extending beyond the algorithmic restrictions imposed by some existing lower bounds. We consider objectives with an $L$-Lipschitz continuous joint gradient, a compact convex dual domain of Euclidean radius at most $D_Y$, and a primal value function, defined by maximizing the objective over the dual variable, with initial suboptimality at most $Δ$. The target accuracy $\varepsilon$ is measured by the gradient norm of the Moreau envelope of the constrained primal value function with parameter $1/(2L)$. Under an unbiased stochastic first-order oracle with variance at most $σ^2$ and mean-squared smoothness, we prove the lower bound $Ω\!\left(L^2D_YΔ\varepsilon^{-3}+L^3D_Y^2Δσ^2\varepsilon^{-6}\right)$. This result quantifies the dependence on accuracy, dual-domain radius, and oracle noise even when variance reduction is allowed. We also establish complementary lower bounds for nonconvex--strongly-concave minimax optimization. With dual strong-concavity parameter $μ>0$ and condition number $κ:=L/μ$, we obtain $Ω\!\left(LΔ\sqrtκ\,\varepsilon^{-2}+LΔκσ^2\varepsilon^{-4}\right)$ under the bounded-variance oracle model. Under the additional mean-squared smoothness condition with constant $\bar L$, we obtain $Ω\!\left(LΔ\sqrtκ\,\varepsilon^{-2}+Δ\bar Lσκ^{3/2}\varepsilon^{-3}\right)$. Together, these results identify complexity barriers across the concave and strongly concave regimes, with the main nonconvex--concave bound remaining valid for algorithms that use variance reduction.

Machine Learning.title: ReFrame: Silence-Aware Compute Reclamation for Full-Duplex Speech Models
Machine Learning.summary: Full-duplex speech models execute dense model inference for every audio frame throughout a live interaction. This uniform framewise schedule creates sustained GPU load across dialogue states whose computation has strong, reusable temporal structure. ReFrame formulates full-duplex inference as a silence-aware computation problem. Mutual Silence Speculation (MSS) operates when both participants are silent: it evaluates multi-frame Temporal continuations, verifies text and hidden-state stability, and applies batched Mimi audio-token correction. Listening Frame Folding (LFF) operates while the user speaks and the agent listens: it processes already-arrived user frames through parallel Temporal execution and frame-batched audio-token generation while accepting only the verified prefix. Frame-Budget Reinvestment (FBR) assigns the released frame intervals to resumable external retrieval and language-model workers, then injects timely references through Moshi's conditioning interface. We instantiate ReFrame on five full-duplex models spanning Moshi-family, phase-structured, and flattened autoregressive generation. Across the complete 1,225-conversation FDBench, ReFrame reduces measured GPU execution time by 18.80-31.01% and retains 96.92-100% non-PAD text agreement on five different models. On HaluEval tests, FBR increases the number of correct generated spoken answers from 86 to 205 under the same auxiliary-service budget. ReFrame turns recurring dialogue structure into lower inference cost and higher end-to-end service capability.

Machine Learning.title: When Should LLMs Be Less Specific? Selective Abstraction for Reliable Long-Form Text Generation
Machine Learning.summary: LLMs are widely used, yet they remain prone to factual errors that erode trust and limit adoption in high-risk settings. One approach to mitigate this risk is to equip models with uncertainty estimation mechanisms that abstain when confidence is low. However, this binary "all-or-nothing" approach is excessively restrictive in long-form settings, often discarding valuable information. We introduce Selective Abstraction (SA), a framework that enables LLMs to trade specificity for reliability by selectively reducing the detail of uncertain content. We formalize SA through selective risk and coverage, and propose Atom-wise Selective Abstraction, a claim-level instantiation that decomposes responses into atomic claims and replaces uncertain atoms with higher-confidence, less specific abstractions. We develop a novel end-to-end pipeline for evaluating long-form generation that instantiates risk as factual correctness and measures coverage as retained information. Our comprehensive empirical evaluation across five LLMs and two long-form factual benchmarks shows that atom-wise SA consistently improves the risk-coverage trade-off, outperforming seven baselines, including claim removal, self-revision, sampling-based aggregation, and chain-of-verification. It improves AURC by up to 35.61% over claim removal, demonstrating that reducing specificity boosts reliability while preserving substantial information. We further provide a risk-guided procedure for selecting a confidence threshold that satisfies a target risk.

Machine Learning.title: Reinforcement Learning with Markov Risk Measures and Multipattern Risk Approximation
Machine Learning.summary: For a risk-averse finite-horizon Markov Decision Process, we introduce a special class of Markov coherent risk measures, called mini-batch measures. We also define the class of multipattern risk-averse problems that reduce to linear MDPs in the risk-neutral case. We use both concepts in a feature-based $Q$-learning method with multipattern $Q$-factor approximation and we prove a high-probability regret bound of $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\big(d^{3/2}HN^{H-1}\sqrt{K}\big)$, where $d$ is the number of features, $H$ is the horizon, $N\ge2$ is the mini-batch size, $K$ is the number of episodes, and $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}$ hides logarithmic factors. We also propose an economical version of the $Q$-learning method that streamlines the policy evaluation (backward) step. The theoretical results are illustrated on a stochastic assignment problem and a short-horizon multi-armed bandit problem.

Machine Learning.title: When Does Latent Prediction Error Support Physical Surprise Claims in Video World Models?
Machine Learning.summary: Prediction errors from video world models are often treated as physical surprise, but they can also reflect appearance, static content, motion, or ordinary prediction difficulty. We present an evaluation framework that separates what frozen representations contain, how they organize appearance and physical differences, and what changes a model's own prediction error. On IntPhys2, a benchmark of physically possible and impossible events, we compare representations from latent prediction, masked pixel reconstruction, and simple visual statistics. Appearance remains easy to decode, while V-JEPA2 exposes modest information about whether events are possible or impossible. Looking at the latent geometry, appearance changes become smaller compared with differences between videos, their directions line up more consistently across scenes, and their overlap with physical changes decreases in deeper layers. Across action-conditioned models, incorrect actions raise prediction error, while appearance changes also produce substantial responses. In Physion++ video clips, repeating a single frame can produce higher error than the original clip, while changing color throughout the clip can lower it. Using Kubric, a simulation and rendering framework, we find that impossible events can produce lower error than possible events. A fixed error threshold also incorrectly flags many possible events as impossible. A model can therefore represent physical information and respond to incorrect actions without its native prediction error reliably measuring physical surprise.
Machine Learning.comment: 28 pages, 12 figures, 25 tables. Accepted at the World Models in Physical AI Workshop, NeurIPS 2026

Machine Learning.title: Domain-Aware Hierarchical Federated Learning for UAV Swarms Across Heterogeneous Environments
Machine Learning.summary: Hierarchical federated learning (HFL) enables communication-efficient training in unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) swarms, but performance degrades under changing and heterogeneous environments. This paper proposes domain-aware HFL (DA-HFL), integrating mobility-informed clustering, cluster-level aggregation, cloud-based Fisher-weighted merging, a domain-adversarial shared backbone, environment-specific heads, and gated inference with local adaptation. A mission-weighted optimization formulation incorporates energy, latency, and cluster-head eligibility constraints. Theoretical analysis establishes resource feasibility, a conditional backbone-stationarity bound, the quadratic optimality of Fisher-weighted merging, and communication and computation complexity bounds. Simulations across four heterogeneous environments demonstrate faster convergence, improved accuracy during environmental transitions, and more stable, purer clusters than the evaluated baselines, with modest energy overhead over resource-aware HFL. Ablation studies validate the contributions of the proposed components.

Machine Learning.title: Learning AI Agents, Market Makers, and Stress in Automated Markets
Machine Learning.summary: Automated markets increasingly route order flow from learning trading agents through automated market makers (AMMs). We model trader archetypes as AI agents defined by their reward functions and analyze the feedback they create on a constant-product AMM. Herd-dominated and arbitrage-dominated markets of equal size have identical return distributions and turnover, so no rule based on volatility, value-at-risk, stress frequency, or volume can tell them apart; yet their stress episodes differ in length by a factor unbounded in the feedback-to-noise ratio $β/s$. Serial statistics identify the feedback sign from $Θ((s/β)^2\log(1/δ))$ observations, and this rate is tight. When agents trade together, profit-seeking agents ride herds rather than lean against them, leading to all-or-nothing participation. Spread-earning market makers restore stability but make liquidity fragile, with discontinuous collapse and hysteresis; maker--taker pricing, not a uniform fee, is the effective instrument.

Machine Learning.title: Detection Instead of Inversion: T1-T2 Microstructure Quantification With Detection Transformers
Machine Learning.summary: T1-T2 correlation MRI has strong potential to quantify microstructural compartments without imposing a biological model. Traditionally, full T1-T2 spectra per voxel are reconstructed with an ill-conditioned and time-consuming Inverse Laplace Transform. We propose to view this challenge as an object detection task: A Detection Transformer (DETR) takes 64 TI/TE signals and directly predicts a set of compartments specified by T1, T2, and signal fraction. We achieve a mean average precision mAP@10 of 76.8% on simulated data, outperforming both our previous model design (53.8%) and regularized NNLS (66.1%). We show that our DETR approach outperforms NNLS in almost every setting across compartment count, compartmental signal fraction, and SNR. Reconstruction is orders of magnitude faster than NNLS. The results are fully reproducible from our public code: github.com/SebastianEndtTHI/t1t2-detr
Machine Learning.comment: 4 pages, 3 figures, 1 table; For submission to IEEE ISBI 2027; Code: https://github.com/SebastianEndtTHI/t1t2-detr

Machine Learning.title: Validity-Gated Evaluation of Multimodal Machine Unlearning
Machine Learning.summary: Machine unlearning aims to remove the influence of training data without retraining a model from scratch. Evaluation of vision-language models relies on forget accuracy (FA), retain accuracy (RA), membership inference, and similarity to a retain-only reference, but evaluation pipelines are rarely tested. We propose a validity-gated unlearning audit (VGUA) with three checks: the forget set must be memorized without duplicate leakage into the retain set, the scorer must measure correctness, and the training code must implement the intended procedure. Applying these checks reveals that random MMBench splits leak duplicate questions, a lenient scorer hides memorization, and two coding errors remove the signal while training completes. After correcting these problems, we evaluate 234 unlearned models using six methods, three learning rates, and three backbones. Each model is compared with a retain-only reference trained using low-rank adaptation (LoRA). The results depend on update strength. Among models with RA at or above 0.70, lower FA generally indicates closer agreement with the retrained FA-RA operating point. Aggressive updates overshoot this point, collapse RA, and reverse method rankings. Relative to the original model, 78% of healthy models move closer to the retrained model's scores, whereas 94% move farther from it in activation space. Membership-inference advantage does not reliably track retraining alignment. Under option-shuffled training, unlearned models answer 25% of reordered forgotten ScienceQA questions, compared with 6% for the retain-only reference. These results show that multimodal unlearning conclusions depend on pipeline validity, update strength, and the comparison criterion.

Machine Learning.title: Acceptance Cards:A Four-Diagnostic Standard for Safe Fine-Tuning Defense Claims
Machine Learning.summary: Safe fine-tuning defenses are often endorsed on the basis of a held-out gap reduction, but the same reduction can come from sampling noise, subject artifacts, capability loss, or a mechanism that does not transfer. We introduce Acceptance Cards: an evaluation protocol, a documentation object, an executable audit package, and a claim-specific evidential standard for safe fine-tuning defense claims. The protocol checks statistical reliability, fresh semantic generalization, mechanism alignment, and cross-task transfer before treating a gap reduction as a full-card pass. Re-scored under this installed-gap protocol, SafeLoRA fails the full-card pass on Gemma-2-2B-it: under strict mechanism-class coding it fails all four diagnostics, and under a permissive shrinkage relabel it still fails three of four. This is a narrow installed-gap audit on one model family, not a global judgment of SafeLoRA's effectiveness. In a 46-cell audit, no cell satisfies the strict conjunction. The closest family is a near miss that passes reliability and mechanism checks where the required data are available, but fails the fresh-subject threshold, lacks a strict transfer pass, and carries a measurable deployment-accuracy cost.
Machine Learning.comment: Because the validation and scope of the four-diagnostic pass rule (deployment capability, cross-task criterion, mechanism diagnostic) and the breadth of the empirical audit do not support the claims as stated. The SafeLoRA result is a narrow out-of-domain stress test, not a judgment of the method. The work is being revised

Machine Learning.title: Improving Sampling Efficiency in RLVR through Adaptive Rollout and Response Reuse
Machine Learning.summary: Group relative policy optimization (GRPO) trains large language models with verifiable rewards by normalizing rewards within response groups. When every response in a group receives the same reward, the advantages vanish and the group provides no policy gradient signal. We propose Adaptive Rollout and Response Reuse Policy Optimization (AR3PO) to obtain informative groups with fewer generations. Adaptive rollout samples responses to each prompt in stages and stops sampling once the model generates a correct response. If all sampled responses are incorrect, response reuse replaces one of them with a past correct response to the same prompt, when available, and recomputes the group advantages. Policy-recomputed reuse trains on the updated groups using probabilities recomputed under the rollout policy; advantage-only reuse uses historical responses only to compute advantages. Across four mathematical benchmarks with 7B and 8B models, AR3PO consistently improves over GRPO and achieves performance comparable to DAPO while requiring up to $4.2\times$ fewer generated responses. Experiments with a 32B model also show comparable performance to DAPO at a similar training stage with substantially fewer generated responses.

Machine Learning.title: MedFL-Stress: A Systematic Robustness Evaluation of Federated Brain Tumor Segmentation under Cross-Hospital MRI Appearance Shift
Machine Learning.summary: Federated learning lets hospitals train segmentation models without sharing patient data, but standard evaluation reports one number: mean Dice across all sites. That number can look competitive while one hospital runs far behind the rest. Our results suggest this gap is not primarily a federation problem. Under controlled MRI appearance shift on BraTS 2020, even a centralised model trained on all data (single seed) shows a 0.055 best-worst client gap. Under FedAvg, federation adds a further 0.030 on top of that. In our setup, appearance shift accounts for most of the gap and federation widens it. We test five methods - centralised, FedAvg, FedProx, FedBN, and q-FedAvg - under this protocol. q-FedAvg achieves the best worst-client Dice in both full-data and subsampled regimes while also maintaining the highest mean Dice among FL methods: no accuracy-fairness tradeoff in our setting, though its margin over FedAvg is not significant at five seeds (p=0.436). FedProx significantly lowers the worst client across five seeds (p=0.019). Worst-client rankings are identical across both evaluation regimes, but FedBN's worst-client spread across seeds is nearly double FedAvg's - a reliability gap that single-seed evaluation cannot see. MedFL-Stress packages this stress test as a reproducible protocol. The main practical message: report worst-client Dice and confirm rankings across evaluation regimes before drawing conclusions from any FL benchmark.

Machine Learning.title: Spectral Signatures of Memorization Basins in Diffusion Trajectories
Machine Learning.summary: Diffusion models are known to reproduce individual examples from their training data as a form of memorization with implications for generalization, privacy, and downstream use. Recent work demonstrated that memorized training samples reside inside contiguous regions of the data/latent space known as basins of memorization -- once a denoising trajectory enters a basin, under finite perturbations it irreversibly reproduces a memorized example. Prior empirical work on such basins in trained models has primarily focused on classifier-free guidance based detection and mitigation strategies in text-to-image models, leaving basin entry and their formation largely uncharacterized. In this paper, we present a geometric characterization of memorization basins for conditional, unconditional, and rectified-flow-based diffusion models. We observe a characteristic signature in the local spectrum of the function geometry that distinguishes basin entry: the emergence of a dominant singular mode followed by a sharp spectral recovery. This signature appears at two timescales: along denoising trajectories during inference and over the course of training. We further investigate whether these geometric signatures can be used to intervene on memorization. During training, we suppress memorization by acting on the dominant mode. At inference, we develop methods to identify trajectories entering memorization basins and steer them away. We find that these interventions remain effective even with low-dimensional approximations of the underlying geometry, and demonstrate that geometry-informed steering extends to large-scale text-to-image diffusion models. Together, our results corroborate that local spectral geometry provides a common basis for characterizing memorization and for suppressing, detecting, and steering away from it across training and generation.

Machine Learning.title: Muon with Nesterov Momentum: Heavy-Tailed Noise and (Randomized) Inexact Polar Decomposition
Machine Learning.summary: Most first-order optimizers treat matrix-valued parameters as vectors, ignoring the intrinsic geometry of hidden-layer weights in neural networks. Muon addresses this mismatch by updating along the polar factor of a momentum matrix, but its theoretical understanding has lagged behind practice. In particular, practical implementations incorporate Nesterov momentum, compute the polar factor only approximately, and operate with stochastic gradients that may be heavy-tailed. We close this gap by developing a convergence theory for Muon with Nesterov momentum and inexact polar decomposition in non-convex matrix optimization under heavy-tailed noise. Our analysis builds on a unified framework for inexact polar decomposition that captures practical iterative approximations such as Newton-Schulz and quantifies how their errors propagate through the optimization dynamics. Under uniform bounds on polar errors, we establish an optimal iteration and sample complexity of $O \left(\varepsilon^{\frac{-(3α-2)}{(α-1)}} \right)$ for finding an $\varepsilon$-stationary point, where $α\in(1,2]$~denotes the heavy-tail index. For the inexact-polar setting with $σ_1=0$, we also provide guarantees that do not require prior knowledge of $α$. We analyze a randomized low-rank polar decomposition that is substantially more efficient than full-space methods while remaining compatible with our theory. Numerical experiments further demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed inexact and randomized~variants.

Machine Learning.title: Silent Reward and Environment Defects in EV Charging Simulation Benchmarks: A Diagnostic Checklist
Machine Learning.summary: Reinforcement-learning (RL) benchmarks built on microscopic traffic simulators such as SUMO are increasingly used to compare agent architectures for electric vehicle (EV) charging assignment. Unlike crashes, defects in the reward function, the environment's stochastic model, or the state encoding often fail silently: the simulation completes, produces plausible numbers, and the comparison is biased. We report five such defects, found by auditing a five-agent benchmark on OpenStreetMap road networks, stated generically: a shared random generator that desynchronises seed-paired comparisons, an ablation-specific reward clip applied unconditionally, a normalisation mismatch that zeroes a reward term, a per-timestep penalty that should fire once per event, and a state dimensionality documented but never wired into the network. We quantify three: a rejection counter inflated up to 125x across agents/cities, a reward term bounded at about $10^{-4}$ of its intended scale, and a 16.6%/16.3% greedy-action divergence from a state-encoding mismatch. Re-analysing a historical ablation, no A1-A2 effect survives family-wise correction; a 56-run campaign confirms the RNG defect's mechanism directly while showing its correction does not change that conclusion. We provide an eight-item checklist as a low-cost first-pass audit; in a later regeneration, three checks caught two new defects while three further process/artefact defects fell outside its boundary.
Machine Learning.comment: 14 pages, 2 figures. Accepted for publication in Bulletin of Electrical Engineering and Informatics (BEEI), ISSN 2089-3191, e-ISSN 2302-9285 (accepted 8 September 2026; in press)

Machine Learning.title: Optimization Frameworks & Learning Algorithms for Discrete-Time Mean Field Games
Machine Learning.summary: This monograph introduces discrete-time mean field games with finite state and action spaces, emphasizing optimization formulations and learning algorithms. Starting from Markov decision processes and finite-player stochastic games, it develops the notion of mean field Nash equilibrium, establishes existence and uniqueness results under suitable assumptions, and explains how mean field equilibria yield approximate equilibria in large finite-player games. Building on the linear programming formulation of Markov decision processes, occupation measures and primal-dual formulations connect equilibrium computation with mathematical optimization. The monograph presents fixed-point iterations, fictitious play, online mirror descent, and optimization-based methods, discussing their convergence properties and limitations. Numerical examples illustrate crowd motion, traffic routing, epidemic management, and the computation of multiple equilibria. It combines examples, theoretical results, and implementable algorithms, with bibliographic notes providing connections to the broader literature.

Machine Learning.title: ReCoG: Relative Node Contexts for Multi-Domain Graph Pre-training
Machine Learning.summary: The success of foundation models in language and vision has motivated Graph Foundation Models (GFMs), which learn transferable knowledge through multi-domain graph pre-training. Existing methods advance GFMs through feature unification and structural learning, and in doing so they rely on the raw graph structure to organize node contexts. However, we observe that removing a large proportion of edges from source graphs during pre-training improves cross-domain transfer accuracy across four representative methods. Our theoretical analysis identifies the raw graph structure as a source of conflict in cross-graph model sharing. We therefore advocate defining node contexts using criteria consistent across graphs. Achieving this requires (1) constructing node contexts consistently across graphs without a shared positional structure, such as the token order of text or the pixel grid of images, and (2) retaining the structural and neighborhood information of the original graphs. To this end, we introduce Relative Contexts for Graphs (ReCoG) for multi-domain graph pre-training. Specifically, we first construct attribute contexts to provide a comparison rule independent of the raw graph structure. Furthermore, we construct structural contexts based on common neighbors and semantic contexts based on neighborhood attribute summaries to retain the topological and neighborhood information of the original graphs. Since all graphs share these construction rules, we pre-train a single graph encoder by reconstructing node attributes over these contexts, without domain-specific modules. We conduct extensive experiments on 18 target datasets, which demonstrate the effectiveness of ReCoG. In particular, ReCoG exceeds the strongest baseline by 7.61 percentage points in mean 1-shot cross-domain node classification accuracy and by 4.47 points in cross-type transfer to heterophilous graphs.

Machine Learning.title: A Deep Reinforcement Learning Framework for Real-Time Electric Vehicle Charging Management in IoEV-Enabled Smart Cities
Machine Learning.summary: The rapid growth of electric vehicles (EVs) in urban environments demands intelligent, decentralised charging management strategies that operate under strict real-time constraints. This paper proposes an Edge-Intelligent architecture in which each EV selects a charging station (CS) by querying a shared, centrally trained Deep Q-Network (DQN) policy over a lightweight MQTT publish-subscribe backbone; independent per-EV edge inference is the deployment target, not the configuration evaluated here. The reported simulation evaluates that shared DQN policy applied sequentially to each vehicle's observations within a single SUMO run, using MQTT for KPI telemetry while observations are obtained through TraCI. The system is evaluated on two real-world road networks from OpenStreetMap (Rabat Agdal-Hay Riad and Tangier, Morocco); the primary network carries four geolocated public charging stations with heterogeneous power levels (50 kW and 150 kW). Three traffic demand profiles (morning, midday, evening peak) are simulated, and four decision policies are compared: an Adaptive Heuristic, a Tabular Q-Learning agent, the proposed DQN agent, and a Double DQN variant. A multi-seed statistical protocol (7 seeds, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, Cohen's d) evaluates the results. The DQN agent achieves a 6.8% relative improvement in charge rate and a 5.4% increase in delivered energy over the Adaptive Heuristic under Evening Peak demand ($p = 0.016$, Cohen's $d = 0.99$ and $1.51$), while showing no advantage in waiting time; on the second network the heuristic leads on waiting time, so the ranking is not stable across geographies. A scalability analysis shows linear state-space growth with station count and sub-millisecond inference; all runs include intermittent station outages under a Markov failure process.
Machine Learning.comment: 17 pages, 4 figures. Authors' accepted manuscript (paper ID 733916, AI2SD 2026 cycle), to appear in an indexed Springer Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems volume. Earlier preprint version deposited on Zenodo: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22208979

Machine Learning.title: Evolving Memory, Learning to Meta-Control: Test-Time Adaptation for Experience-augmented LLM Agents
Machine Learning.summary: Self-evolving agents accumulate experience from task streams, but existing frameworks typically rely on fixed pipelines to retrieve and utilize this experience, neglecting when and how to deploy it. We introduce Online Meta-Control of Experience (OMCE), a framework that updates experience memory and learns a meta-control policy from task feedback during test-time adaptation. OMCE employs a lightweight contextual-bandit meta-controller that uses compact retrieval signals to select among four cognitive actions: DIRECT, EPISODE, GUIDE, and DISTILL. This routing mechanism operationalizes three coupled decisions: whether to invoke experience, which memory format to utilize, and when to consolidate new guidance. OMCE evolves online, leveraging task feedback to update the memory bank and refine the routing policy via contextual bandit updates. Experiments on four online adaptation benchmarks across four backbones show that OMCE improves first-attempt success by up to 20.5 percentage points over the strongest compared baseline, while reducing per-task token use by a factor of 5.7 to 62.5 relative to ACE with GPT-5.2. Controlled ablations further support the benefits of learned routing and continued routing policy adaptation.
Machine Learning.comment: 23 pages, 5 figures. Submitted to ACL Rolling Review (October 2026)

Machine Learning.title: Convex Regression at Scale: Geometry-Preserving Constraint Sparsification
Machine Learning.summary: Convex regression provides a flexible nonparametric estimation framework while incorporating appropriate shape information. However, its standard least-squares formulation has $O(n^2)$ supporting-hyperplane constraints creating a computational bottleneck as the sample size $n$ increases. We study a $K$-nearest-neighbor (KNN) localized relaxation for convex regression where we for each sample, we only maintain the $K$ nearest hyperplane constraints. Under mild regularity conditions, we establish statistical guarantees for our modified estimator in every fixed dimension $d\ge2$. In particular, for $d>4$, the population risk of our modified problem can be shown to have equivalent convergence rates as the original least square convex regression estimator of $\widetilde O(n^{-2/d})$ using neighborhoods sizes (i.e. $K=K_n$) of order $\widetilde O(n^{2(d-1)/(2d-1)})$ for general convex functions and $\widetilde O(n^{(d+1)/(d+2)})$ for strongly convex functions. To corroborate our theory, we implement iterative optimization methods to compare the prediction accuracy of the KNN relaxation with those of the full estimator across synthetic convex benchmarks. Our experiments demonstrate that KNN prediction risk approaches the full-estimator prediction risk at neighborhood sizes matching the theoretical scale.

Machine Learning.title: How Does Chain-of-Thought Supervision Teach Models to Reason? A Theoretical Analysis
Machine Learning.summary: Training with chain-of-thought (CoT) supervision is an effective approach for teaching models multi-step reasoning procedures. At inference time, however, models may need to continue reasoning beyond the finite teacher CoT sequences observed during training, and longer reasoning can instead degrade performance, a phenomenon known as overthinking. How the amount and structure of training-time CoT give rise to such failures remains theoretically poorly understood. To study this problem, we introduce an in-context weight prediction model trained on finite gradient descent trajectories for linear regression. Using high-dimensional asymptotic analysis, we show that the success and failure modes of long-horizon reasoning undergo phase transitions depending on the context length and the total amount of training CoT. We further distinguish two mechanisms of overthinking, error accumulation and error amplification, and show that with short training contexts, increasing the training CoT budget can worsen long-horizon error before eventually stabilizing reasoning. Experiments with fully trained linear and multi-head softmax attention further show that these qualitative behaviors persist. Our results provide a theoretical account linking properties of training-time CoT to inference-time failures and offer guidance for designing teacher CoT that supports stable reasoning.

Machine Learning.title: CacheWeave: Learning to Recompute for Efficient Position-Independent KV Caching
Machine Learning.summary: Position-independent caching reuses chunk KV caches across positions and requests. Independent encoding, however, omits cross-chunk interactions and can degrade accuracy. In our study, neither PIC training nor rule-based recomputation, alone or combined, consistently recovers full-prefill accuracy. Oracle-guided recomputation on PIC-trained models improves accuracy at the same budget, motivating better selection. We present CacheWeave, which adapts the full backbone to PIC, then freezes it and trains a model-native block selector on the adapted model's oracles. The selector uses compact cached chunk features and question hidden states without extracting backbone attention scores. It selects contiguous token blocks aligned with KV blocks to support efficient recomputation and limit copy-on-write amplification. Its runtime, CacheWeave-Serve, supports private and shared KV caches, keeps selection and recomputation on the GPU, and stages sliding-window KV for hybrid attention models. Across three models and four tasks, CacheWeave outperforms CacheBlend and ProphetKV by 7.2 and 3.5 percentage points on average at a 5% recomputation budget, with a mean relative accuracy loss of 1.6% to full prefill. With 32-token blocks, CacheWeave-Serve cuts single-request TTFT by up to 16.1x over full prefill and 1.7x over ProphetKV, and raises SLO goodput under load by up to 7.8x.

Machine Learning.title: Robust EEG-based Emotion Recognition from Coarse Trial-level Labels under Intra-trial Affective Variability
Machine Learning.summary: EEG-based emotion recognition has become an active research area in brain-computer interfaces. However, fine-grained affective annotation is costly, so most datasets provide only a global label for each long EEG trial. For practical emotion recognition, trials are commonly divided into short temporal windows, with the global label propagated to all windows for training. This practice treats trial-level emotion as temporally uniform, although affective responses may fluctuate within a trial. Consequently, windows that weakly reflect or deviate from the global emotional state may receive unreliable labels, posing a key challenge to robust EEG-based emotion recognition. To address this challenge, we propose VARY, a variability-aware robust learning framework for EEG-based emotion recognition from coarse trial-level labels. VARY incorporates a Two-stage Sample Selection (TSS) strategy to identify EEG windows with reliable emotional labels, and introduces MixAug, a data augmentation method tailored for EEG to improve model robustness under limited and unreliable supervision. We comprehensively evaluate VARY under the setting of label-noise learning on two public datasets, using three network architectures and multiple label-noise settings. Our method demonstrates superior performance, achieving a maximum accuracy gain of 11.54% on the DREAMER dataset and 5.39% on the SEED dataset compared with the best-performing baseline, highlighting the effectiveness of VARY in learning from unreliable trial-level labels under intra-trial affective variability.

Machine Learning.title: Beyond Imputation: Mask-Adaptive Conformal Prediction via Tree Embeddings on General Missing Data Mechanisms
Machine Learning.summary: Conformal prediction (CP) provides a distribution-free framework for uncertainty quantification with finite-sample marginal coverage guarantees. Yet, missing values introduce distributional heterogeneity, where marginal coverage can hide systematic undercoverage for certain missingness patterns. At the same time, existing methods based on distances or smoothness require a continuous representation of partially observed covariates. Although imputation restores continuity, it obscures the missingness patterns and introduces task-dependent overhead. We develop a new CP framework that is \emph{adaptive to missingness patterns}, without imputing covariates. We rely on data augmentation by feature embedding that accounts for missingness. Our framework represents each input with missing values by a tree embedding together with its raw missingness mask, and then learns a regularized quantile score function. Varying the choices for the penalty function and the augmentation enables us to characterize three practically relevant validity levels: exact coordinate-wise validity, exact validity on observed masks, and approximate missingness-conditional guarantees for general mechanisms (MCAR, MAR, MNAR). Experiments on synthetic and real datasets support these guarantees and show that the proposed method reduces miscoverage risk while maintaining informative intervals, especially in non-MCAR settings. These results highlight the practical value of uncertainty quantification that adapts to missingness.

Machine Learning.title: A sensor-driven physics-informed neural network for real-time occupant-centric space heating control
Machine Learning.summary: Conventional space heating systems typically rely on single or sparse fixed-point temperature measurements, overlooking non-uniform indoor temperature distributions, transient thermal dynamics, and occupant-specific comfort requirements. This study explores an occupant-centric control strategy that aims to maintain the desired temperature around the occupant location. Spatially and temporally varying temperature fields, together with occupant mobility, make real-time local temperature estimation challenging. To address this challenge, we propose a control-oriented Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) model for indoor temperature-field prediction. Conventional PINNs rely on explicit time inputs and assume consistent temporal patterns across samples, which limits adaptability under variable initial conditions and heating sequences. The proposed model infers temporal dynamics implicitly from spatial coordinates and limited sensor measurements, improving robustness to changes in initial conditions and external disturbances. The method was validated across nine horizontal sensing planes in three controlled room-scale configurations. Against a validated COMSOL Multiphysics simulation, the PINN predicted the evaluated temperature fields with a maximum relative error below 1.85% across validation cases. These predictions supported an occupant-centric space heating control scheme. Compared with COMSOL-based offline control, the PINN-based system achieved an average prediction error of around 0.67%, and its rapid inference supports real-time occupant-centric control implementation. This work represents a move away from reliance on fixed-point temperature measurements in space heating control to an occupant-centric control strategy informed by real-time environmental feedback.

Machine Learning.title: Mean Field Reinforcement Learning: Theory and Algorithms for Mean Field Control
Machine Learning.summary: This monograph provides an introduction to mean field reinforcement learning through the lens of Markov decision processes arising from large-population stochastic control with mean field interactions and common noise. Starting from the connection between multi-agent reinforcement learning and mean field control, it develops the probabilistic, mathematical, and control-theoretic framework needed to formulate representative-agent learning problems, analyze their relationship with finite-population systems, and study both general and linear-quadratic models. The presentation includes dynamic programming principles, propagation-of-chaos limits, and theoretical analyses of tabular Q-learning and policy-gradient methods. It also discusses numerical implementations, including tabular schemes and deep reinforcement learning methods such as deep deterministic policy gradient. The goal is to give readers a coherent bridge between mean field control theory and reinforcement learning methodology, emphasizing the mathematical structure of the problems and the design of tractable learning approaches for large stochastic populations.

Machine Learning.title: Mask-Conditional Conformal Prediction: Valid Uncertainty For All Missing Data Mechanisms
Machine Learning.summary: Conformal prediction (CP) offers a principled framework for uncertainty quantification, but it fails to guarantee mask-conditional coverage when faced with missing covariates. In addressing the heterogeneity induced by various missing patterns, Mask-Conditional Valid (MCV) Coverage has emerged as a more desirable property than Marginal Coverage. In this work, we adapt split CP to handle missing values by proposing a preimpute-mask-then-correct framework that can offer valid coverage. We show that our method provides guaranteed Marginal Coverage and Mask-Conditional Validity for general missing data mechanisms. A key component of our approach is a reweighted conformal prediction procedure that corrects the prediction sets after distributional imputation (multiple imputation) of the calibration dataset, making our method compatible with standard imputation pipelines. We derive two algorithms and prove that they achieve both marginal validity and MCV. We evaluate them on synthetic and real-world datasets. It reduces significantly the width of prediction intervals w.r.t standard MCV methods, while maintaining the target guarantees.
authors: Juhyun Park. Thi Phuong Thuy Vo

Machine Learning.title: When Disagreement Labels Do Not Identify F1 Rankings
Machine Learning.summary: Agreement labels cancel from an accuracy comparison but can change an F1 ranking. We specialize partial identification to an explicit audit after labeling disagreements: two agreement counts give exact bounds, certifying a ranking or a choice within a specified F1 tolerance under every completion. Across 3,200 frozen model pairs, shared completions tighten bounds and a 0.01 tolerance reduces labeling costs. A zero-loss (weak-winner) control attributes most savings to positive tolerance, not ties. Guarantees concern the evaluated batch, not future data.
Machine Learning.comment: 6 pages, 1 figure, 1 table. Submitted to ESANN 2027, submission ES2027-34. Code and reproducibility artifact: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23647323

Machine Learning.title: Comparative Strategies for Handling Imbalanced QSAR Regression: A Case Study on hERG Activity Prediction
Machine Learning.summary: Data imbalance frequently occurs in QSAR modeling, yet most studies focus on classification tasks, and few address regression tasks, as it is challenging to determine which regions of the data are sparse or dense. Data-level and algorithm-level imbalance-handling strategies can have different effects on model performance. In this study, we systematically compare various strategies across GCN and fingerprint-based machine learning models. To evaluate model performance more meaningfully, we partitioned the target region into several subregions based on both domain knowledge and data distribution. We focused on the region of greatest practical interest. Our results demonstrate that selecting models based on this interest-region metric leads to more reliable performance than using the total region metric. We also observed that different imbalance-handling strategies can have divergent effects depending on the model type. These findings highlight the importance of region-aware evaluation in regression QSAR modeling and provide practical guidance for selecting appropriate strategies for imbalanced datasets.

Machine Learning.title: Adaptive Auto-Harness: Sustained Self-Improvement for Agentic System Deployment on Open-Ended Task Streams
Machine Learning.summary: Auto-harness systems improve LLM agents by adapting prompts, skills, tools, and supporting infrastructure from execution feedback. Sustaining these gains on open-ended task streams requires handling growing histories, heterogeneous tasks, and shifting distributions. We introduce Adaptive Auto-Harness, a unified framework that separates persistent evolution workspaces from deployable harnesses and supports interchangeable evolution procedures. We compare configurations adapted from five prior approaches on recorded streams of prediction markets, security challenges, and event forecasts. With the same Sonnet solver, our full system reaches 80.9\% market all-task accuracy and 50.2\% security Pass@1, versus 22.2\% and 37.2\% without evolution; market accuracy also exceeds a market-following control's 72.0\%. Our analyses show that artifact accumulation does not guarantee sustained gains, and knowledge that transfers across tasks can still lose value as the task distribution changes. Continued evolution can therefore help preserve earlier gains through revision of accumulated knowledge. Code: https://github.com/A-EVO-Lab/a-evolve.

Machine Learning.title: MatMoE: Matryoshka Mixture-of-Experts with Dynamic Mixed-Precision Quantization for Efficient Inference
Machine Learning.summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture has been widely adopted in large language models (LLMs) since it reduces the computational cost through sparse expert activation. However, the massive parameter scale of MoE models hinders their deployment on resource-constrained edge devices. Although existing mixed-precision quantization reduces the model size, they are inherently static, fixing the bit-width of each expert across decoding steps. Such static schemes yield suboptimal performance as they overlook the dynamic variation in expert importance during decoding. Furthermore, they fail to adapt to the dynamic latency constraint driven by the fluctuating system utilization. To address these challenges, we propose MatMoE, a dynamic mixed-precision quantization framework for efficient MoE inference. MatMoE features: (1) a Matryoshka MoE PTQ algorithm that enables experts to operate flexibly at multiple precisions within a stringent memory budget; (2) a floor-and-compensation quantization method that eliminates redundant memory accesses in the Matryoshka representation; and (3) a dynamic bit-width allocation strategy that determines the precision for each expert based on their routing scores to satisfy the dynamic latency requirement. We implement our MatMoE system atop llama.cpp for both CPU and GPU platforms. Extensive evaluations across three modern MoE models and challenging benchmarks demonstrate that MatMoE achieves $4.0\% \sim 18.3\%$ higher accuracy than state-of-the-art static mixed-precision method. Compared to llama.cpp, MatMoE delivers $1.3\times \sim 3.7\times$ speedup on Raspberry Pi 5, and $1.2\times \sim 1.3\times$ speedup on NVIDIA RTX 4090 and Jetson AGX Orin.

Machine Learning.title: SparseLift: Automatically Optimizing Opaque Sparse Paths in Industrial-Scale Recommendation Model Training
Machine Learning.summary: The sparse path, comprising sparse operations and collective communication, is a critical component of large-scale recommendation models. However, these operations are often represented as opaque nodes in the training computation graph, hindering whole-graph optimization. We present SparseLift, a low-overhead compiler for the sparse path of large-scale recommendation training. It exposes sparse computation and communication to whole-graph analysis to expand the optimization space and improve training efficiency. By analyzing model structure and runtime information, SparseLift reconstructs opaque nodes as analyzable subgraphs, recovering the resource semantics of sparse computation and communication within the graph. Building on the recovered semantics, we design incremental cost models and a constraint-aware planner to automatically select and organize subgraph optimizations into an execution plan that is reused during subsequent steady-state training. We evaluate SparseLift on an industrial video-platform recommendation task with 100B sparse parameters and the public DLRM benchmark. SparseLift improves steady-state throughput for ordinary industrial training steps by 16.5\% over the native baseline. On DLRM, it achieves $1.60\times$ and $1.26\times$ model-execution speedups over DLRM-Baseline and TorchRec, respectively.

Machine Learning.title: Certifiable inversion of resampling-induced spectral distortion in high-dimensional particle filters
Machine Learning.summary: This paper formulates and solves the inverse problem of recovering the pre-resampling spectrum of a particle filter's ensemble covariance from the importance weights and the observed spectrum alone. Resampling controls weight degeneracy, but in high dimensions it also distorts that spectrum: the distortion is a free multiplicative convolution with a law computable from the weights, so the repair is a deconvolution. We first extend the forward spectral law to random importance weights by conditioning on the weights together with the realized offspring counts rather than on the weights alone, which makes the distortion law deterministic at the observed data and gives the zero-atom mass of the limiting law a direct reading as an effective-dimension proxy for the second-order information the filter has lost. Second, a regularized free deconvolution inverts the distortion with an explicit error budget at a fixed resolution scale, and a computable forward residual certifies when the model behind it is violated. Injectivity makes the inverse identifiable but not stable, so the budget rests on a resolution-restricted condition number whose positivity we prove, and is vacuous below that resolution rather than concealed in a hypothesis. Third, the repaired spectrum enters only as the preconditioner of a Metropolis-adjusted rejuvenation move, so spectral error changes the mixing constants and not the invariant target, and the full cycle obeys a geometrically summable error recursion whose abstention term is governed by when abstentions fall rather than how many occur. Pre-registered simulations confirm the forward law, an order-of-magnitude reduction of spectral error, and the abstention law. The repair recovers eigenvalue laws, not eigenvectors.
Machine Learning.comment: This is a preprint of an article submitted to Inverse Problems. The implementation and experiment scripts are available at https://github.com/songming-teaching/spectral-repair-resampling. This is the second paper in a series on spectral analysis of particle filters. The first paper is available at arXiv:2610.16680

Machine Learning.title: Direct Covariance-to-Beamformer Mapping for Low-Latency Hybrid ISAC Beamforming with Subsequent DoA Estimation
Machine Learning.summary: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) systems typically employ a two-stage beamforming pipeline, in which target directions are first estimated from the received covariance matrix and then used to compute the beamforming weights by solving non-convex optimization problems. Although effective, this approach introduces processing latency that can limit beam adaptation in dynamic environments. This letter proposes a beamforming deep neural network (BFDNN) for direct covariance-to-beamformer learning in ISAC systems. BFDNN is a compact regression network that maps covariance-matrix features directly to the hybrid beamforming weights produced by a hybrid ISAC beamformer, eliminating the direction-of-arrival (DoA) estimation stage during inference. Compared with MUSIC, classification-DNN, and regression-DNN based beamforming pipelines, BFDNN generates comparable beam patterns and higher effective spectral efficiencies while reducing the beamforming prediction latency by 25-30 times on the evaluated platform, demonstrating the potential of direct covariance-to-beamformer learning for low-latency ISAC beam updates. Moreover, the target directions can be inferred indirectly from the generated radiation pattern, yielding DoA accuracy competitive with that of dedicated learning-based methods in the evaluated scenario.

Machine Learning.title: HARN: Hierarchical Associative Resonance Network for Event-Driven Multi-Timeframe Forecasting
Machine Learning.summary: Live financial forecasting must synchronize asynchronous bar completions across timeframes without using stale or unavailable information. We introduce HARN (Hierarchical Associative Resonance Network), an event-driven architecture that anchors each event to the finest configured timeframe and maintains persistent states and matrix-valued associative memories across temporal levels. Its timestamp-masked transition updates a level only when its completed-bar timestamp matches the current anchor, preserving inactive representations. HARN integrates causal multi-scale encoding, residual-driven gated associative writes, all-to-all cross-level resonance, and ordered bottom-up evidence aggregation to produce forecasts at each temporal level. Predictions are expressed as basis-point changes and reconstructed on the price scale for evaluation. We evaluate HARN on four assets spanning equities, foreign exchange, and gold (AAPL, EURUSD, USDCHF, and XAUUSD), using chronological 70/15/15 splits, 32-bar lookbacks, one-step horizons, and three random seeds. HARN obtains lower anchor-timeframe test mean absolute errors (MAEs) than the evaluated single-timeframe PatchTST and TimeXer baselines on all four assets. HARN's MAEs are 0.508, 0.000306, 0.000263, and 2.552, respectively; PatchTST records 2.074, 0.000759, 0.000638, and 9.563, while TimeXer records 2.882, 0.010838, 0.014144, and 15.297. These descriptive comparisons do not isolate architectural effects from differences in inputs, target formulations, or training procedures. Single-run component ablations on AAPL and EURUSD show small, non-monotonic differences. The results demonstrate HARN's feasibility for asynchronous multi-timeframe forecasting, while motivating controlled comparisons and broader ablations to establish its relative advantages and component contributions.

Machine Learning.title: SEALECT: Scene-Conditioned Pose Priors for Plausible Maritime Vessel Retrieval
Machine Learning.summary: We address scene-conditioned object retrieval for compositional augmentation in maritime imagery, where strong geometric constraints make appearance-only retrieval produce physically implausible vessel insertions. We propose SEALECT, a retrieval framework that jointly models visual compatibility, vessel pose, scale, and scene geometry through a unified score combining neural similarity, scene-conditioned pose priors, and observed-pose consistency. We construct a maritime scene-pose library and model the pose and scale priors nonparametrically, as a kernel that conditions each prior continuously on the scene with no learned parameters. Across seven maritime benchmarks, our trained scene-conditioned retriever exceeds the strongest appearance encoder (SigLIP 2) in recall (+0.14), and the training-free prior raises geometric plausibility further at negligible recall cost, more than halving the constraint violations of appearance retrieval and outperforming learned foreground-search baselines (GALA-style, DiscoFOS). In a blind study of end-to-end composites (BootPlace placement, DiffHarmony harmonization), SEALECT ranks first among six methods, ahead of random and GALA-style selection and statistically tied with CLIP, DiscoFOS, and DINO.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted to WACV 2027 (Applications Track). 22 pages: 11-page main paper including references, plus 11 pages of supplementary material. Code: https://github.com/fossil-ai/SEALECT

Machine Learning.title: Stabilizing Consistency Training: A Flow Map Analysis and Self-Distillation
Machine Learning.summary: Consistency models have been proposed for fast generative modeling, achieving results competitive with diffusion and flow models. However, these methods exhibit instability and limited reproducibility when training from scratch, motivating subsequent work to explain and stabilize these issues. While these efforts have provided valuable insights, the explanations remain fragmented, and the theoretical relationships remain unclear. In this work, we provide a theoretical examination of consistency models by analyzing them from a flow map-based perspective. This joint analysis clarifies how training and convergence behavior can give rise to degenerate solutions. Building on these insights, we revisit self-distillation as a practical remedy for certain forms of suboptimal convergence. To avoid excessive gradient norms during its optimization, we reformulate its objective empirically, yielding improved Self-Distillation (iSD). We further extend iSD with training-time classifier-free guidance, yielding iSD-T, which improves performance and reproducibility in the studied settings. We demonstrate that iSD extends beyond image generation to diffusion-based policy learning, without reliance on pretrained diffusion models for initialization.

Machine Learning.title: Mosquito acoustic identification at unseen recording sites: practical limits of common transfer remedies for vector surveillance
Machine Learning.summary: Passive acoustic monitoring could widen mosquito surveillance, but a classifier trained under one set of recording conditions often fails when moved to a new site, device or enclosure. On a nine-species, five-condition corpus of about 271,000 recordings, the published baseline identifies species at 0.881 balanced accuracy under conditions it has seen and 0.175 under held-out ones. Using that corpus's leave-domain protocol, we asked which transfer strategy is most reliable when a program brings a new site online. Using fixed features from a pre-trained bioacoustic model and a small classifier improved held-out-condition balanced accuracy to 0.305, without updating backbone weights and in minutes of training per site. Four widely used additions did not improve transfer: rebalancing training across recording conditions, fine-tuning the backbone and fusing a weaker second modality each reduced accuracy, and a six-term objective reduced to a single alignment term. Rebalancing reversed direction across four encoders, helping weak representations and harming strong ones. Genus-level aggregation was more accurate than species-level classification (about 0.50 against 0.30), suggesting genus-level screening may be the more realistic operating point here. These results come from one corpus under one protocol, and are dataset-bounded guidance rather than validated general rules.
Machine Learning.comment: Major revision: reframed from a domain-generalisation study to an acoustic monitoring study. All Perch results re-measured in a single environment, five seeds; two claims now rest on paired seed-for-seed tests rather than interval overlap. 38 pages, 5 figures

Machine Learning.title: StretchTime: Adaptive Time Series Forecasting via Symplectic Attention
Machine Learning.summary: Transformer architectures have established strong baselines in time series forecasting, yet they typically rely on positional encodings that assume uniform, index-based temporal progression. However, real-world systems, from shifting financial cycles to elastic biological rhythms, frequently exhibit "time-warped" dynamics where the effective flow of time decouples from the sampling index. In this work, we first formalize this misalignment and prove that rotary position embedding (RoPE) is mathematically incapable of representing non-affine temporal warping. To address this, we propose Symplectic Positional Embeddings (SyPE), a learnable encoding framework derived from Hamiltonian mechanics. SyPE strictly generalizes RoPE by extending the rotation group $\mathrm{SO}(2)$ to the symplectic group $\mathrm{Sp}(2,\mathbb{R})$, modulated by a novel input-dependent adaptive warp module. By allowing the attention mechanism to adaptively dilate or contract temporal coordinates end-to-end, our approach captures locally varying periodicities without requiring pre-defined warping functions. We implement this mechanism in StretchTime, a multivariate forecasting architecture that achieves state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks, demonstrating superior robustness on datasets exhibiting non-stationary temporal dynamics.

Machine Learning.title: Leveraging 2D Foundation Priors for Generalized Category Discovery under Test-Time Adaptation in 3D LiDAR Segmentation
Machine Learning.summary: In autonomous driving, 3D LiDAR semantic segmentation is expected to adapt to evolving environments and recognize previously unseen categories, making generalized category discovery under test-time adaptation (GCD-TTA) an important problem. However, existing works treat GCD and TTA separately, while the limited semantic information in 3D point clouds makes GCD-TTA under domain shift more prone to feature collapse when combining GCD with TTA. To address this issue, we propose a two-stage framework for GCD-TTA in 3D LiDAR semantic segmentation. Specifically, in the first stage, we adaptively aggregate local 3D features according to geometric density variations and obtain reliable pseudo labels under a global class-wise prototype consistency constraint. In the second stage, we cast category discovery as an optimal transport assignment process for globally consistent grouping of novel categories. Meanwhile, semantic features from 2D vision foundation models are fused with 3D point cloud features to enrich 3D semantic information and promote a more separable feature space. Extensive experiments on Synth4D to SemanticKITTI, SynLiDAR to SemanticKITTI, and Synth4D to nuScenes demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework. Under a unified evaluation protocol, our method achieves the best overall mIoU on 9 out of 10 benchmark splits and improves the overall mIoU by up to 12.21 points over the strongest re-implemented baseline.

Machine Learning.title: Wave Physics as Representation: Tensor-Structured Neural Reconstruction for Ocean Acoustic Fields
Machine Learning.summary: Reconstructing three-dimensional (3D) complex ocean acoustic fields from sparse measurements is challenging due to highly oscillatory wave structures and restricted sensing patterns/routes. Learning-based approaches fall into two categories. First, purely data-driven models can learn complex field patterns, but do not explicitly exploit wave physics that may enhance interpretability and reduce training costs. Second, physics-informed methods impose a specified physical equation as a reconstruction constraint, but often require environment-dependent parameters that are difficult to acquire. As a result, practical 3D acoustic field reconstruction that is both physically grounded and robust to uncertain environmental information remains largely unexplored. This work takes an alternative route: instead of solving a fully specified wave equation, it extracts a structured representation from wave physics and learns its components from data. From the Helmholtz equation and normal mode propagation, we derive a structured spatial-angular tensor representation, termed the S/c representation. Under a low-rank specialization, it takes the form of a rank-(L,L,1) block-term tensor decomposition, which connects structured sampling patterns/routes used in ocean sensing to sufficient conditions for field recovery. Building on this tensor representation, we propose TIDAL, a neural reconstructor that uses the S/c representation as an inductive bias for structured decoding and aligns information aggregation with the sampling geometry. The neural learner removes the need for known model parameters required by conventional physics-based recovery methods. Experiments across three structured sampling geometries show that TIDAL achieves the best reconstruction performance and fastest inference among baselines, with benefits from the physics-derived representation under limited data and model capacity.

Machine Learning.title: Xiaomi Auto World Model 2.0: Causal World Models for Real-World Driving and Embodied Intelligence
Machine Learning.summary: We present Xiaomi Auto World Model 2.0, a unified streaming causal world model for Physical AI. It models and generates causal physical evolution in the real world, and unifies heterogeneous conditioning inputs for view-consistent generation. The architecture integrates View-Temporal Attention (VTA) to capture cross-view spatial dependencies and temporal dynamics, together with Multi-view Rotary Position Encoding (RoPE) to encode positional relationships across views and time. WorldRec 2.0 reconstructs static and dynamic 3D Gaussians from multi-view, multi-temporal observations in a single forward pass and uses their renderings as explicit scene context to preserve geometry and appearance during long-horizon generation. Conditioning inputs are fused through VAE latent concatenation in a shared representation space. We incorporate Gated Linear Attention (GLA) into the temporal layers of VTA for efficient streaming inference, reducing computation and KV-cache memory during multi-view rollouts. A physical-interaction data pipeline covers diverse interactions and long-tailed events. From Pre-train onward, these data are combined with large-scale videos and heterogeneous visual modalities to learn visual, geometric, and dynamic priors. During Mid-train, training across diverse view configurations further improves the model's ability to capture how actions and object states shape subsequent scene evolution. After distillation-based Post-train, we apply the model to closed-loop simulation, closed-loop training, and World Action Model (WAM) applications. These applications generate physically consistent future states and support world-state prediction, policy learning, and action generation for Physical AI.

Machine Learning.title: PGID: Progressive Guided Inversion and Denoising for Robust Watermark Detection
Machine Learning.summary: With the proliferation of AI-generated images, digital watermarking has become an essential safeguard for protecting intellectual property and mitigating malicious exploitation. Recent works on semantic watermarking have enabled efficient copyright protection for diffusion models. However, the dependence of semantic watermarking on diffusion inversion for watermark detection creates a critical vulnerability. Imprint removal and forgery attacks exploit this weakness to produce deceptive results. Our analysis reveals that these attacks succeed by displacing watermarked latents into the unwatermarked region, while guiding unwatermarked latents into the watermarked region. Based on that, we propose Progressive Guided Inversion and Denoising (PGID), the first plug-and-play, training-free noise extraction framework designed to defend against both attack strategies. PGID effectively defends by projecting perturbed latents back to the region where they originally belong. The projection is achieved by eliminating intermediate latent deflections and mitigating adversarial perturbations through progressive inversion-denoising cycles. Comprehensive evaluations across multiple schemes demonstrate that PGID successfully restores detection reliability by recovering removed watermarks and identifying forged instances.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026. Code available at https://github.com/MinhQDuong/PGID

Machine Learning.title: How Much Does Random Rotation Help GPTQ? Sharp Worst-Case Rate Gaps in the High-Rate Regime
Machine Learning.summary: GPTQ is Babai's nearest-plane algorithm on the lattice of the Cholesky factor of the layer's input second moment $Σ$. In the high-rate, entropy-coded regime it needs $\tfrac12\log_2(\AM/\GM)$ of its Cholesky pivots more bits than WaterSIC, which is within $0.255$ bit of the rate-distortion limit for every $Σ$; random rotations close most of this gap in practice, and Ordentlich and Polyanskiy asked for the worst-case gap between rotated GPTQ and WaterSIC. We show that after a Haar rotation the $k$-th pivot converges almost surely, uniformly in $k\geδn$ and over spectra $ν$ of bounded condition number, to $1/S_ν(-k/n)$, a classical formula from the theory of Lyapunov exponents, and use it to answer the question. Over spectra with condition number $κ$ the worst rotated gap is $\tfrac12\log_2κ-\log_2\lnκ+\tfrac12-\tfrac1{\ln2}+o(1)$ bits, attained only by two-point spectra, just $\tfrac12\log_2\lnκ+O(1)$ bits below the worst case without rotation, so rotation cannot replace waterfilling in general. It nearly can on real layers: rotation cuts the cost of an $η$-fraction of outlier eigenvalues of size $μ$ from about $ημ$ to $η^2μ/2$ to leading order, but cannot remove spectral spread on a logarithmic scale; for non-Gaussian weights it also adds a weight-side rate cost, which we characterize exactly under a standard high-rate assumption. On $96$ Hessians of Qwen3 and Llama-3.1 the rotated gap has median $0.04$ bit and maximum $0.36$ bit, against $2$--$5$ bits in the worst case for the same condition numbers, and the limit matches it to within $0.009$ bit.

Machine Learning.title: Stand-In Effects and Pooling Amplification: Design-Based Tests of Whether Biological World Models Use Actions
Machine Learning.summary: Action-conditioned world models are increasingly trained on data from randomized experiments, and whether their predictions respond to actions is usually checked by replacing or removing the actions and measuring the loss in accuracy. We show that such diagnostics report action effects where there are none: under autocorrelated designs, future actions stand in for history the model does not see, and a better model learns the stand-in better. When the design law is known, a conditional randomization test written as an e-value is valid in finite samples whatever the model, provided the resampler conditions on the full state the design used; resampling from a simpler law reproduces the false effect. We identify a second failure, specific to world models: when many sites share one action sequence (cells in a microscope field, pixels in a frame), the natural pooled score turns small model errors along the action contrast into overwhelming evidence against a true effect. In a pixel world, its median log e-value fell from $-17.3$ to $-6832$ as frames grew from 64 to 4096 pixels, while the oracle's rose. Tempering the score by a design effect estimated on training data changes the bet, not the validity. Our own preregistered analysis of optogenetic ERK experiments failed in exactly this way; a tempered statistic, selected on synthetic data and registered before the data were obtained, then rejected the null on a never-opened field ($E\approx 1.1\times10^{10}$). Every analysis is preregistered, fixed in a dated protocol before it was run, or labelled exploratory, and every reported result is generated from hashed result files.
Machine Learning.comment: 54 pages, 6 figures, 24 tables. Preregistrations: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/ZXAR3 (M4) and https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/QEZBX (M5). Primary category cs.LG: a test for learned action-conditioned models; cross-listed for the statistical method (stat.ME) and the biological application (q-bio.QM)

Machine Learning.title: A Hybrid Anomaly Detection Method for Multivariate Time Series
Machine Learning.summary: Multivariate time series are ubiquitous in monitoring smart systems such as power plants, smart houses, and servers. These systems use multiple sensors to collect the system's status over time. Those sensors represent the status of the whole system as one entity. Anomaly detection in such smart systems is of critical importance to prevent system failure and maintain functionality. But anomaly detection in such multivariate time series data is very challenging since this type of data includes both temporal and spatial information. Capturing both of these pieces of information is important to detect anomalies. In this paper, we propose a hybrid deep learning-based anomaly detection method, which captures both temporal and spatial information. We propose to take advantage of the feature extraction capabilities of 2d convolutional network in a variational autoencoder, alongside a prediction-based deep neural network of 2d convolutional networks and a gated recurrent unit network to capture both spatial and temporal information. Experiments on public data against state-of-the-art show the potential of our method.

Machine Learning.title: A Hybrid Anomaly Detection Method for Electric Vehicle Identification from Smart Meter Recordings
Machine Learning.summary: In recent years, electric vehicles (EVs) have attracted much attention due to their potential to decarbonize the transport system. EV charging imposes challenges on power grids, such as load imbalance and voltage instability. Therefore, electricity distributors need to identify which users have an EV. Smart meter recordings can be effectively used for this purpose. The major issue associated with such data is the imbalance problem, where the majority of the data belongs to users without EVs. The existing methods for EV identification from smart meter recordings have framed it as a classification task. In this paper, we frame the problem as an unsupervised problem and propose a hybrid anomaly detection method that combines the power of prediction-based and reconstruction-based anomaly detection methods. The proposed model considers temporal and stochastic representation information of smart meter time series via prediction-based and reconstruction-based components, respectively. The performance of the proposed model is compared with state-of-the-art supervised and unsupervised methods. Its superiority is verified on real-world data.

Machine Learning.title: Inference for Batched Adaptive Experiments
Machine Learning.summary: The advantages of adaptive experiments have led to their rapid adoption in economics, other fields, and among practitioners. However, adaptive experiments pose challenges for causal inference. This note suggests a BOLS (batched ordinary least squares) test statistic for inference on treatment effects in adaptive experiments. The statistic provides a precision-equalizing aggregation of per-period treatment-control differences under heteroskedasticity. The combined test statistic is a linear combination of heteroskedastic per-period z-statistics and can be used to construct asymptotically valid confidence intervals. We provide simulation results comparing rejection rates in the typical case with few treatment periods and few (or many) observations per batch.

Machine Learning.title: Physics-Informed One-Step Generation on Long-short flow maps
Machine Learning.summary: Physics-informed generative models should produce samples that are both data-aligned and physically valid, yet existing methods are often iterative and too slow for practical use. Achieving this with a one-step flow-map model is difficult because both data-distribution and physics-constraint learning are enforced only indirectly through surrogate objectives, making their joint learning fragile for long-range flow maps. We propose \textbf{Physics-Informed Long-Short Flow Maps with Direct Guidance (LSFM-DG)}, which makes direct target computation feasible by decomposing one-step generation into a long flow map for global evolution and a near-terminal short flow map with computable closed-form solutions and physics potentials. As the short flow map shrinks to zero, it provides both direct distributional and physical targets for learning the long flow map. This yields a unified one-step flow-map model that removes Jensen's gap, improves training stability, and achieves stronger data fidelity and physical consistency without distillation.

Machine Learning.title: Near-Optimal $\sqrt{K}$-Regret for Online Learning in Uninformed Markov Games
Machine Learning.summary:
We study online learning in two-player uninformed Markov games, where the opponent may follow an arbitrary, unknown policy in each episode and the learner does not observe the opponent's actions. [TWYS21] showed that achieving sublinear external regret requires an exponential dependence on the episode length $H$. Motivated by this limitation, they studied the weaker notion of Nash-value regret and obtained an $\widetilde{O}(K^{2/3})$ regret bound, where $K$ is the number of episodes.
